articles.title: No hate for Lacson amid ‘witch hunt’ vs Taguig projects – Cayetano
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Senate minority leader Alan Peter Cayetano said he holds no grudges against Sen. Panfilo Lacson as the latter, in Cayetano’s words, supposedly subjects Taguig City to a…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Senate minority leader Alan Peter Cayetano said he holds no grudges against Sen. Panfilo Lacson as the latter, in Cayetano’s words, supposedly subjects Taguig City to a “demolition job, witch hunt and trial by publicity.”
Cayetano, in a Facebook livestream on Wednesday, talked about the improvement projects in Taguig in the last 15 years.
Some of these constructions are being scrutinized and investigated by Lacson who said that Cayetano funded “ghost” deals.

“Yes, I am openly saying that Senator Panfilo Lacson is carrying out a demolition job, a trial by publicity, and a witch hunt in Taguig City,” Cayetano began. “I have no problem being accused. I am a public official.”

He continued: “But he is linking all the projects to Taguig and to me, all the titles there. It’s not only unfair, but it’s just plain wrong. If he can’t convince people, he will try to confuse people.”
Cayetano insisted that he is not upset with Lacson, urging his supporters to instead “hate the sin, but love the sinner.”
“I have no anger. No hatred towards Senator Lacson,” he expressed.
Cayetano then promised to “give clarity” to Lacson’s reports against the Taguig projects.
He is also encouraging the public to visit the parks, public areas and flood control infrastructure in his turf that have supposedly developed in the past decade and a half.
In Cayetano and Lacson’s most recent dispute, Lacson said that there are at least P3.7 billion in public funds that may have been “wasted” in projects in the reclamation areas of Taguig City.
Cayetano, in response, told Lacson to let investigative offices probe into the Taguig projects.
Lacson, on the other hand, said he had turned over to the Office of the Ombudsman his office’s findings on the Taguig City infrastructure projects. /apl

articles.title: Over 11,000 classrooms damaged by habagat, cyclones — DepEd
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Rains and floods from the southwest monsoon or ‘habagat,’ and recent tropical cyclones have affected over 11,000 classrooms nationwide, the Department of Education said on…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Rains and floods from the southwest monsoon or ‘habagat,’ and recent tropical cyclones have affected over 11,000 classrooms nationwide, the Department of Education said on Wednesday.
Nationwide, the combined effects of the southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones damaged 2,243 schools and 11,167 classrooms.
The DepEd said it requires an estimated P7.783 billion in funds, including P65.036 million for immediate cleanup and clearing operations.
Funds include P319.97 million for minor repairs in 1,487 schools and P1.194 billion for major repairs in 669 schools.
Additionally, the DepEd needs P5.62 billion to reconstruct 490 heavily damaged school sites.
Of these, 6,530 classrooms sustained minor damage, 2,389 suffered major damage, and 2,248 were totally damaged.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara and President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. inspected damaged areas in Tarlac, Zambales, and Pampanga on Wednesday.“We are immediately allocating the necessary assistance for the repair of schools, while ensuring the safety and well-being of our teachers and students,” Angara said in a statement.

Data from DepEd’s Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Service showed that Central Luzon sustained the heaviest damage from the combined effects of the southwest monsoon and recent tropical cyclones.
At least 622 schools and 4,025 classrooms were affected in Central Luzon.
The damage included 946 classrooms totally destroyed, 806 with major damage, and 2,274 with minor damage.
DepEd estimated that Central Luzon would require P2.9 billion for response and recovery efforts.
This includes P19.49 million for cleanup, P111.43 million for minor repairs, P402.5 million for major repairs, and P2.37 billion for reconstruction.
A total of 1,748 classrooms in 442 schools nationwide are currently serving as temporary shelters for 13,723 displaced families.
As of Sept. 1, 367 public schools nationwide had suspended face-to-face classes due to the effects of the monsoon and tropical cyclones. INQ /mr

articles.title: ‘Hindi mayabang’: Low incomes leave Filipinos little to save
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — An economist pointed out that many Filipinos are struggling to save because their incomes are barely enough to make ends meet, leaving little — or nothing — to spare. Sonny…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — An economist pointed out that many Filipinos are struggling to save because their incomes are barely enough to make ends meet, leaving little — or nothing — to spare.
Sonny Africa stressed that “millions of Filipinos consume all their earnings and don’t save because their incomes are so low that they don’t have anything left to save.”
He said this in response to Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Eli Remolona Jr., who cited Filipinos’ “consumption culture” as one reason the peso sank to its weakest level on record.

“Mahirap sabihin ‘to, Senator, pero mayabang tayo. Maano tayo, may consumption culture ang tawag,” Remolona said Thursday, Aug. 27, during a Senate hearing on whether the peso can still regain its value.
“It’s a bit difficult to say this, Senator, but we tend to like showing off. We have what you call a consumption culture.”

However, Africa, executive director of Ibon Foundation, said that “telling 96 million Filipinos that their ‘consumption culture’ is the problem is astoundingly entitled, and bordering on willful ignorance.”

Based on the think tank’s estimate, 70 million Filipinos belong to the poorest and low-income classes. They earn an average of no more than P10,000 and between P10,000 and P22,000 a month, respectively.
Some 26 million Filipinos are in the lower-middle-income class, earning an average of P22,000 to P36,000 a month.
High cost of living
Ibon Foundation earlier pointed out that Filipinos are already struggling with the high cost of living as prices of basic goods and services rise faster than their wages and incomes.
Salaries, it said, have “barely moved,” noting that the average minimum wage rose by only P31, from P481 to P512.
“This is nowhere near enough to cover the average family living wage, estimated by Ibon Foundation at P1,277 a day for a family of five and P1,533 for a family of six,” it said.

blocks.caption: GRAPHIC: Ed Lustan/INQUIRER.net

blocks.text: The Philippines recorded a poverty incidence of 9.7% in 2025, bringing the share of Filipinos living below the government’s poverty threshold to a single-digit rate, the Philippine Statistics Authority said.

But while this technically fulfilled President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s promise to end his six-year presidency with a 9% poverty incidence, the think tank slammed what it described as “outdated, unrealistic” standards.
The 2025 annual per capita poverty threshold was P35,121, or P96.22 per person per day. For a family of five, this translates to only P14,434 a month.
Less intention to save

The BSP’s latest Consumer Expectations Survey indicates that households’ intention to save dropped sharply from April to June, months before the southwest monsoon and a series of typhoons brought prolonged rains that led to widespread flooding.
The Saving Intention Index fell to -0.7 from 12.4 in the first three months of the year, according to Dr. Alicor Panao, Inquirer data scientist and University of the Philippines associate professor.
The index compares households intending to save more with those expecting to save less. A negative reading indicates that more households anticipate a decline in their savings than an increase.

Panao said the index had been deeply negative for most of 2022 to 2024 before improving through 2025 and turning positive late last year. The optimism continued into early 2026, only to reverse after the first three months.

For Africa, “it’s easy for someone earning P53 million a year to say this — huwag maging mayabang (don’t be showy), save more,” pointing out that Remolona is the highest-paid government official in the Philippines.

“That’s about 130 times what the average Filipino family earns. It’s also more than what the central bank governors of Australia, England, Japan, US, Taiwan, India, and the European Central Bank are paid,” he said.

Africa explained that “instead of victim blaming,” Remolona should think more about “how to drive cheap finance towards poor farmers and fisherfolk, towards MSMEs building a genuinely Filipino industrial base, and towards providing affordable public social services, infrastructure, and utilities.”
INQUIRER.net sought Remolona’s comment on Africa’s remarks but had not received a response as of posting time.
Low savings rate
The BSP explained that the country’s savings rate remains low, contributing to the weaker value of the peso.
The Inquirer sought comment from the BSP, but the central bank provided only World Bank data on the country’s gross savings.
According to the data, the Philippines’ gross savings stood at 26%, lower than Indonesia’s 36%, Vietnam’s 38%, Cambodia’s 40%, Brunei’s 44% and Singapore’s 48%.
Remolona earlier said, “As much as possible, hopefully our savings will increase,” noting that this is the “long-term solution [to the peso’s depreciation].” /dm

articles.title: Poa maintains no involvement in DepEd confidential funds during Sara Duterte's term
articles.summary: Atty. Michael Poa on Wednesday maintained that he had nothing to do with the confidential funds of the Department of Education (DepEd), despite serving as the agency"s chief of staff and…

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 6:24pm

Atty. Michael Poa on Wednesday maintained that he had nothing to do with the confidential funds of the Department of Education (DepEd), despite serving as the agency’s chief of staff and undersecretary while Vice President Sara Duterte was Education secretary.
On the 21st day of Duterte’s impeachment trial, Poa said documents showed that responsibility for handling the confidential funds rested with a special disbursing officer and a security officer.

“I understand the people who are asking, who are thinking, ‘Imposible naman na hindi niya alam, COS siya.’ But anyone who has worked with the Vice President would know that when she runs an office, it’s highly compartmentalized. Ibig sabihin, kung anong binigay sa iyo na function, ’yun lang ang tututukan mo,” he said.

(I understand the people who are asking and thinking, ‘It’s impossible that he didn’t know about the confidential funds because he was the chief of staff.’ But anyone who has worked with the Vice President would know that when she runs an office, it’s highly compartmentalized. That means you focus only on the function assigned to you.)
“Kung tatandaan natin, ’yung confidential funds, it started way before I became chief of staff,” he added.
(If we recall, the confidential funds started way before I became chief of staff.)
Poa served in several capacities at DepEd under Duterte, including as spokesperson, undersecretary, and chief of staff.
During her interpellation, Senator-Judge Imee Marcos asked Poa: “So maliwanag na maliwanag para sa iyo na ’yung confidential funds, hindi mo trabaho ’yun kahit COS ka ng Secretary?”
(So, it is very clear to you that handling the confidential funds was not part of your job, even though you were the Secretary’s chief of staff?)
Poa, who had been declared a hostile witness by the Senate impeachment court, answered in the affirmative.
Security officer
Poa also disclosed during the trial that he was unaware that DepEd had a security officer to whom former special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda turned over confidential funds in 2023.
Poa said he learned about the functions of Col. Dennis Nolasco only during a House panel hearing in October 2024.

“Si Col. Nolasco actually, hindi ko siya nakita sa DepEd nung mga panahon na nandoon ako. Hindi ko siya kilala at all. Si Col. Lachica, to be fair, kilala ko po siya kasi nag-courtesy call siya as the commander of the VPSPG,” he said.

(I actually didn’t see Col. Nolasco at DepEd during my stint there. I didn’t know him at all. To be fair, I do know Col. Lachica because he paid a courtesy call in his capacity as commander of the VPSPG.)

During the 2024 House inquiry, Fajarda told lawmakers that he released P4 million to P6 million a week in confidential funds to a “security officer” designated by a colonel from the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSPG).

Xylene del Campo of the Commission on Audit (COA) previously recalled that during the 2024 hearing, Fajarda said Duterte instructed him to turn over the confidential funds to Nolasco for disbursement.
Del Campo said the move violated Joint Circular 2015-01, which governs the use of confidential and intelligence funds. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Tehran attacks U.S. bases across Gulf after reports of deadly strike on wedding
articles.summary: Iran and its Arab neighbours were plunged back into war on Wednesday by the biggest exchange of fire between Tehran and Washington since July, with U.S. forces striking Iran's southern coast and Iran…

image.caption: Pedestrians walk past a wall mural of Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, along a street in central Tehran on Monday. (Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

Iran and its Arab neighbours were plunged back into war on Wednesday by the biggest exchange of fire between Tehran and Washington since July, with U.S. forces striking Iran's southern coast and Iran firing at American bases across the region.
Latest escalation marks biggest exchange between both countries since July
The United States threatened more devastating strikes. Iran accused Washington of hitting a wedding party, killing five people and wounding dozens.

Asian and European stocks fell after the renewed U.S. airstrikes, which pushed oil prices back up to levels unseen since July, compounding the economic impact of a global sell-off in bonds as disrupted energy supplies fuel inflation worldwide.

The U.S. military's Central Command said it struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps air defences, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites on Tuesday. Iranian media reported hits on multiple targets near the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway where Tehran has threatened tankers attempting to pass without its permission.

Iran responded by striking what it said were U.S. assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq, and said its aim was now to drive U.S. forces out of the vast network of military bases they have maintained for decades across the Middle East.

"American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences," Iran's military command said.
U.S., Iran trade new strikes, warnings as hostilities flare

Jordan's military said it dealt with 13 missiles, 10 of which were intercepted and three which fell in remote areas. The IRGC said it killed a large number of U.S. forces in Jordan, but U.S. officials told Reuters there had not been any casualties, according to initial assessments.

In Kuwait, Iran said it had carried out a missile and drone attack on the vast U.S. Ali Al Salem Air Base and targeted the accommodation of a U.S. commander. Kuwait’s fire service said crews put out a blaze at a residential complex early on Wednesday that was struck by an Iranian drone causing damage but no casualties.

items: Day of attacks by U.S. and Iran marks most serious escalation of conflict in weeks
Iran's Revolutionary Guard retaliates after U.S. bombs targets in Strait of Hormuz

blocks.text: Qatar, home of the largest U.S. airbase in the Gulf, said it holds Iran "fully legally responsible for these attacks and their repercussions and consequences." Bahrain, which houses the regional headquarters of the U.S. navy, said Iranian drones were intercepted and destroyed.

The IRGC said its ground forces carried out combined missile and drone attacks on U.S. bases in Erbil in northern Iraq, claiming to have killed several U.S. personnel there. Neither Iraq nor the U.S. confirmed the attack.
Iran also said two tankers had been struck by mines while being steered across the Strait of Hormuz by U.S. operatives through a channel that Tehran says it has closed.
5 killed during wedding in Iran

Iran reported at least 12 deaths from the night of U.S. strikes, with five people including a four-year-old said to have been killed while celebrating a wedding at a home in Sirik, a town along the coast of the strait.

Iranian media said as many as 68 people were wounded there, and released images of several injured children in hospital. Iranian officials compared the incident to a strike on a girls' school that killed 160 people on the war's first night.

Reuters was unable to independently verify the incident and U.S. officials did not comment on it. Video filmed by Iran's West Asia News Agency at the purported site showed rubble strewn across rooms and a courtyard of a home. A pair of strappy women's dress sandals lay abandoned on a blood-soaked carpet.
"I am just glad the casualties weren't even worse," said Ali Molahi, identified as the father of the bride.
Can Iran really launch sea mines from rockets? | About That

The exchange of fire was the worst since July, when U.S. President Donald Trump abruptly halted two weeks of intense bombing of Iran after warnings from his military brass that they were using up munitions and running out of meaningful targets.

Iran's war-battered economy and degraded conventional forces have left it stretched thin, while Washington has used up much of its stocks of air defense munitions and burned through its precision long-range missiles.

Still, Trump, who has yet to achieve the aims he set when launching "Operation Epic Fury" in February — to end Iran's nuclear program, deprive it of the ability to strike its neighbours and create conditions for Iranians to topple their rulers — repeated his declarations that victory was at hand.

"I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing," he said on Tuesday. "They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?"

Iran, for its part, is determined to humble U.S. forces and emerge from the war stronger than before it, with sanctions lifted, billions in blocked funds released, and its newfound grip over the strait letting it collect fees from ships that carried a fifth of global oil before the war.
Trump agreed to many of Tehran's demands in a June deal, but the ceasefire collapsed within weeks over control of the strait, and no talks between the foes have been held since.

articles.title: Russian airspace becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Ukrainian president says aviation industry needs to take account of growing number of Ukrainian attack drones in Russia
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh in Kyiv and Pjotr Sauer

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Russia’s airspace is becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, as Vladimir Putin promised to step up strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities in the run-up to winter.

The Ukrainian president said there was no intention to directly threaten civilian flights, but the growing number of attack drones being flown into the country by Ukraine would have to be “taken into account” by the aviation industry.
“We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” he said in a statement.
A rapid escalation of Ukrainian military capability in the past few months has allowed the country’s forces to strike locations deep inside Russia.

Reliable figures for the number of drone flights are hard to obtain but Ukraine is already capable of launching several hundred a day, and military sources say the country is chasing a target of 1,000 drones in an effort to hurt Russia’s economy.

Ukraine’s commercial airspace has been closed since the beginning of the full scale invasion in February 2022 because Russia has been able to strike targets throughout the country, making airports unsafe for civilians.

This year, Ukraine has begun bombing oil refineries and warehouses near Moscow and St Petersburg, as well as hitting military and industrial sites at ranges in excess of 2,000km (1,250 miles) from its border.

Concerns about the safety of civilian aviation in the war zone linger. A Malaysian airlines plane was shot down as it flew over eastern Ukraine in July 2014 by Russian separatists operating a surface to air missile launcher. All 298 people onboard were killed.
Putin described Zelenskyy’s remarks as “state terrorism”, saying: “Negotiations are not conducted with terrorists.”

Giving one of his most detailed updates on the war, the Russian leader told a news conference that Moscow was preparing to step up its campaign bombing Ukraine’s energy facilities this winter, aiming to knock out heating and electricity supplies.

“The Russian armed forces have been ordered to prepare and carry out mass strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. They are striking us, and they will get a response,” Putin told reporters after a two-day summit in Kyrgyzstan. “I’m not saying we’ll collapse the economy there, but it’s a serious challenge for them.”

blocks.caption: Putin at a news conference on Tuesday, where he gave one of his most details updates on the war.  Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/EPA

blocks.text: Asked whether Russia would strike British military facilities in the UK that produced weapons for Ukraine, Putin sidestepped the question, saying: “That’s a military secret.”
Russia earlier accused the UK of “escalation” and threatened “consequences” after reports that British-made drones were used by Ukraine in long-range strikes deep inside its territory.

Putin sought to stress that Russian forces retained the initiative on the battlefield in Ukraine, despite Moscow’s slowing progress. He appeared to push back against western intelligence reports suggesting he was being given an overly optimistic picture of the war, saying he relied on numerous sources of information that together provided him with an “objective assessment” of the battlefield.

At one point, however, Putin claimed that Russian forces had captured the Ukrainian town of Sviatohirsk in the Donetsk region. The claim was not supported by battlefield maps produced by DeepState, a Ukrainian monitoring group.

Even some pro-war Russian commentators disputed Putin’s account. “This is simply a lie. Sviatohirsk has not been liberated,” wrote the pro-war blogger Alexei Larkin. “The level of the president’s misinformation is critical.”

Russia’s sluggish advance on the battlefield has fuelled widespread speculation inside the country that the Kremlin could resort to another round of mobilisation, the first since Putin called up about 300,000 reservists in September 2022.

Zelenskyy and western officials have warned that Moscow could be preparing such a move, though its diplomats do not consider it is a certainty. Addressing the speculation for the first time, Putin dismissed the prospect of a new mobilisation as “nonsense”.

The Russian leader also said he was comfortable dealing with Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as part of efforts to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, although he acknowledged talks were “currently frozen, to a certain extent”.
The CIA director, John Ratcliffe, made a rare visit to Moscow last week and reportedly pressed the Kremlin to end the war.

articles.title: Tropical Storm Pilandok may exit PAR on September 3
articles.summary: The enhanced southwest monsoon is affecting Luzon and the Visayas, while the haze from Indonesia is currently affecting western sections of the Visayas and Mindanao

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Tropical Storm Pilandok (Krovanh), which is enhancing the southwest monsoon or habagat, may exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) by early Thursday, September 3.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in its 5 pm bulletin on Wednesday, September 2, that the tropical storm was last located 1,085 kilometers east northeast of extreme Northern Luzon, moving west northwestward at 14 kilometers per hour, with maximum sustained winds of 65 km/h and gustiness of up to 80 km/h.
It still has no direct effect on the country, far from the Philippine landmass, and is unlikely to make landfall, remaining over the northern Philippine Sea as it moves toward Okinawa, Japan.

Tropical Storm Saudel (formerly Obet), meanwhile, was located 460 km west northwest of Itbayat, Batanes, with the same strength as Pilandok’s (winds of 65 km/h, gustiness of up to 80 km/h), moving east northeastward at 20 km/h.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Benison Estareja said Saudel is gradually weakening as it moves toward southern China, and there is a high chance that the tropical storm will no longer enter PAR, although if it does reenter, it would only be for a while and as a tropical depression.
The weather bureau is monitoring another low pressure area (LPA) 2,745 km east of Central Luzon, with a “low” chance of developing into a tropical depression.
These weather disturbances continue to enhance the southwest monsoon or habagat.
Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan are seeing moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters) on Wednesday afternoon due to the southwest monsoon.

The rain will ease in some provinces and affect only Zambales, Bataan, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro on Thursday afternoon before heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm) is seen again in Occidental Mindoro and moderate to heavy rain in Zambales, Bataan, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas, Oriental Mindoro, and Antique on Friday afternoon.
These provinces should watch out for floods and landslides.

The southwest monsoon is also bringing strong to gale-force gusts, especially in coastal and upland areas exposed to winds, over most of Luzon and the Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Oriental, Camiguin, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental, and Davao Oriental.
Moderate to very rough seas will persist in the following areas:
Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

items: Seaboard of Batanes; the northern and western seaboards of Babuyan Islands — waves up to 5 meters high
Seaboards of Ilocos Norte and northern Ilocos Sur — waves up to 4.5 meters high

blocks.text: Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

items: Seaboard of northern La Union; the western seaboard of Pangasinan — waves up to 4 meters high
Seaboard of Zambales; the western seaboard of Bataan — waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboard of Lubang Islands; the northern and western seaboards of Calamian Islands and Kalayaan Islands; the southern seaboard of Bataan; the western seaboards of Cavite, Batangas, and northern Occidental Mindoro; the remaining seaboard of Babuyan Islands — waves up to 3 meters high

blocks.text: Up to moderate seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

items: Seaboards of Isabela and southern Surigao del Sur; the remaining western seaboard of Palawan; the eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental; the remaining seaboards of La Union, Pangasinan, and Kalayaan Islands; the northern seaboard of mainland Cagayan; the remaining western seaboard of Occidental Mindoro — waves up to 2.5 meters high

Seaboards of northern Aurora, Romblon, Cuyo Islands, Cagayancillo Islands, Antique, and Davao Occidental; the southern seaboards of Quezon, Marinduque, Iloilo, and Guimaras; the eastern and southern seaboards of Oriental Mindoro; the western seaboard of southern Negros Occidental; the remaining seaboards of mainland Cagayan, northern Palawan, Occidental Mindoro, Surigao del Sur, and Davao Oriental — waves up to 2 meters high

blocks.text: Due to the southwest monsoon, too, smoke and fine particles from Indonesia are being pulled toward the western sections of the Visayas and Mindanao, resulting in haze as of Wednesday morning, with Mindanao seeing thicker haze than on Tuesday, September 1.
Estareja said the haze started on Sunday, August 30, in Palawan, affecting Metro Manila and nearby provinces in Southern Luzon on Monday, August 31, then Southern Luzon and the Visayas on Tuesday.
PAGASA is seeing improving air quality as the wildfires weaken for now. PAGASA advised those in affected areas to wear N95 or KF94 face masks outdoors, or stay indoors if possible.
Meanwhile, occasional heavy rain and strong winds due to the southwest monsoon and LPAs remain prevalent in September, but easterlies may prevail toward the end of the month, weakened by El Niño.
Two to three tropical cyclones are expected to enter PAR in September. The country has had 16 tropical cyclones so far in 2026, with five to nine more expected in the next four months.
The tropical cyclones in September (to be named Queenie, Rosal, and Samuel) may make landfall over Luzon or enhance the southwest monsoon. – Rappler.com

articles.title: OP's confidential funds have proper documentation, receipts, says Palace
articles.summary: Malacañang on Wednesday defended anew the Office of the President"s (OP) proposed P4.56 billion in confidential funds for 2027, saying that their confidential funds in the past had bulks of receipts.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 6:11pm
Malacañang on Wednesday defended anew the Office of the President’s (OP) proposed P4.56 billion in confidential funds for 2027, saying that their confidential funds in the past had bulks of receipts.

Criticisms against the OP’s confidential funds came as Vice President Sara Duterte is undergoing an impeachment trial over her alleged misuse of the confidential and intelligence funds, among other Articles of Impeachment.

“Kapag nagri-report po ang OP pagdating sa confidential funds ay bultu-bulto po ang mga dokumento at hindi po gumagamit ng mga resibo na maaaring masabing kuwestiyonable,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro told reporters.
(When the OP makes its reports about the confidential funds, the documentation is in bulk and this does not use recruits that could be questionable.)

Earlier, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said the CIF (confidential and intelligence funds) that the Office of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. is seeking constitutes roughly 45% of its proposed P10.15 billion budget for the next fiscal year.

“Number one, the President is the chief executive officer. The President is the head of state, so his first job is to ensure law and order, and diyan ginagastos ‘yung confidential fund (that is where the confidential funds are used),” he said.
“With regard to intelligence funds, he is the commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. ‘Yan naman napakahalaga (that is very important) for our national security,” he added.
Meanwhile, Castro said the OP could easily justify its fund usage to the Senate.
Asked about the former Education Undersecretary Michale Poa taking the witness stand at the impeachment trial, Castro declined to comment.
However, she did raise the previous findings of the House Committee on Good Governance under then chair Rep. Joel Chua.

She recounted how former DepEd Undersecretary Nolasco Mempin had been asked to look for certifications to justify the use of confidential funds to the Commission on Audit. Mempin would be able to secure these from the Armed Forces of the Philippines, with the Youth Leadership Summit being used as an excuse.
“Ang supporting documents ba ay gagamitin lamang para magkaroon ng rason dahil nagastos ang P15 million or dapat mayroon talagang allocated na 15 million for a particular operation?” Castro said,
(Are supporting documents used as a reason to justify spending P15 million or should there be P15 million allocated for a specific program?) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Senate okays bill banning kin of public officials from gov't contracts
articles.summary: The Senate on Wednesday approved on third and final reading a measure seeking to bar relatives of public officials up to the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity from entering into…

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 6:10pm

The Senate on Wednesday approved on third and final reading a measure seeking to bar relatives of public officials up to the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity from entering into government contracts.
With 15 affirmative votes, zero negative votes and zero abstentions, the upper chamber approved Senate Bill No. 1962, authored by Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero, during its plenary session.

Under the measure, relatives of any covered public official or personnel within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity would be barred from participating in or entering into any government contract, as well as from engaging in subcontracting, consortiums, joint ventures or similar business arrangements for the performance of a government contract.
The prohibition covers relatives by blood or marriage up to the fourth degree, including parents, children, siblings, grandparents, grandchildren, uncles, aunts, nephews, nieces and first cousins.

It would apply to contracts between private entities and government agencies or instrumentalities involving supplies, materials, machinery, equipment and services, as well as infrastructure, joint venture and public-private partnership projects and other similar agreements.

The bill also provides that violators may face imprisonment of one to three years, a fine of at least P100,000 and perpetual disqualification from participating in or entering into any government procurement activity.

Public officials or personnel who violate the proposed law may likewise face imprisonment of one to three years, a fine of at least P100,000 and perpetual disqualification from holding public office.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos says PH had flood control master plan for decades: We're executing it now
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. said the country has had a flood control master plan "for decades," but it is only that it is being implemented.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 6:07pm
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. said the country has had a flood control master plan "for decades," but it is only that it is being implemented.
Marcos answered in the affirmative when asked if he was expecting a flood control master plan.

"We already have a masterplan. It’s just never been executed. We are only executing it now. We have had a masterplan for decades, but walang ginawa. Hanggang ngayon lang. Ngayon lang natin sinisimulan," Marcos said.
(We already have a master plan; it’s just never been executed. We’re only executing it now. We’ve had a master plan for decades. But nothing has been done until now; we’re just starting now.)
Marcos said this after inspecting the damaged Agana and Aquino bridges in Tarlac. The bridges collapsed amid flooding and heavy rain caused by the Southwest Monsoon or Habagat.

Malacañang recently announced the plan to build five dams in Nueva Ecija and a 100-kilometer dike extending toward Pilar, Bataan, as part of the government’s long-term solutions to recurring flooding in Central Luzon.
The proposed projects were discussed during a situation briefing in Pampanga last week following widespread flooding in the region.
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said the government is looking at immediate, medium-term and long-term measures to reduce the impact of flooding in Central Luzon.

Immediate measures include the repair of damaged infrastructure, as well as declogging, desilting, and dredging operations. The government will also continue monitoring these interventions to determine whether they remain effective and durable, Castro said.

At a budget hearing on the Department of Public Works and Highways' proposed budget of more than P643 billion for 2027, Secretary Vince Dizon said there was no national plan for flood control and drainage.
What the country has, according to Dizon, are flood control plans for all 18 of the country's major river basins. He said this was the recommendation of the DPWH's foreign partners. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Thousands still missing as Nepal-Tibet flood relief and recovery intensifies
articles.summary: More than 1, 000 people have died and thousands are missing, with communities relying on airlifted supplies.

blocks.text: A massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, wiping out villages.
Nearly 12,000 people have since been rescued, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

But thousands more, including hundreds of foreign nationals - from India, the UK, Australia, the US, Malaysia, and more - are still missing. A week on, fears are growing that the death toll will only rise.

Chinese state media has not reported any survivors on the Tibetan side of the border, but the search continues. Beijing, which annexed Tibet in the 1950s, tightly controls the region. All information comes from state media and foreign journalists cannot travel there without permission.

Rescuers using heavy machinery, working around the clock, have been able to re-open the route to the Gyirong border crossing between Nepal and Tibet and clear the road of debris, which will accelerate the search for the missing, Chinese state media said.

Rescue operations continue in challenging conditions, and experts from China and India are helping build temporary bridges to reach remote areas. Drones are being deployed over hard-to reach areas to scan for survivors.
The UN's humanitarian agency said the main challenge is now access, with more than 40 bridges destroyed.
The most remote communities are relying on army helicopter flights for supplies, and villages are still struggling for fuel and electricity.

The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers.
In Nepal, nearly 3,500 people have been left homeless and displaced in 27 sites - mostly schools, which disrupts education - across the districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa.

The priority for them now is "receiving humanitarian assistance, recovering and identifying the remains of the loved ones, tracing missing relatives and reunifying separated children, and accessing psychosocial support", the UN's humanitarian agency said.
People packed into overcrowded shelters, contaminated water and damaged health facilities are putting the population at greater risk of disease in the middle of the monsoon season, the agency added.
Nepal's prime minister, Balendra Shah, said there was a renewed emphasis on protecting the lives of survivors, providing medical treatment and psychological counselling.
Nepal's government and the UN have agreed to launch a four-month humanitarian flash appeal.

articles.title: US aircraft carrier docks near Thai beach resort Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
articles.summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln is docking close to Pattaya, known for its neon-lit nightlife, and for sex tourism.

blocks.text: US aircraft carrier docks near Thai beach resort Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
Watch: Why do US troops have history with this Thai city?
ByJonathan Head
South East Asia correspondentReporting fromPattaya, Thailand
After a record 250 days at sea without a port stop, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand, giving its nearly 5,000 crew members a much-needed break.
The ship is docking close to the beach resort of Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife and for sex tourism. For the US it also carries strong historical echoes.

When the weary sailors walk into the city's bars and restaurants, they will literally be treading in the footsteps of the hundreds of thousands of US troops who came here for R&R – rest and relaxation - during the Vietnam War.
They transformed it from a sleepy fishing village to one of the world's most famous and frenetic party towns.

Today the neon-lit alleys running down to the beach are much quieter than usual. The bars in the city's famous Walking Street still screen videos on their walls of pole-dancing women, trying to lure customers inside.
But there are not many of those customers, and most seem to be family groups from the Middle East more interested in the Turkish ice-cream vendor than the go-go bars.

The Iran War, which has affected tourism and consumer spending, has hit businesses hard here. The prospect of thousands of American sailors, with nine months of salary unspent while at sea, offers a rare opportunity to local businesses.

blocks.caption: Image caption, US personnel arriving at the Hard Rock Hotel in Pattaya on Wednesday

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
US personnel arriving at the Hard Rock Hotel in Pattaya on Wednesday
The US carrier left San Diego last November on what was supposed to be a six-month assignment in the Pacific and South China Sea.
However, the ship was diverted to the Gulf after the US and Israel began military operations against Iran in late February.

Recently some members of Congress raised concern about reports of food shortages, broken toilets and mental stress among the crew. The US Navy acknowledged that working conditions have been tough, but said the crew were sufficiently well-supported. It would not, however, comment to the BBC on the carrier docking at Pattaya, citing operational security.
Despite its close relationship with China, Thailand is a treaty ally of the US, and port visits by US Navy ships are a familiar occurrence.
But this is probably the largest number of US military personnel coming straight from a war zone to Pattaya since the fall of Saigon in 1975.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pattaya's streets, know for their raucuous nightlife, are quieter than usual

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Lulu Luo
Pattaya's streets, know for their raucuous nightlife, are quieter than usual

"This visit could be our best hope," said Anon Saiteer, who sells gems in a shop near Walking Street, which has put up a large sign welcoming the US sailors and marines and offering them a special discount. "We have nothing to lose – we just hope they will spend some money here."
But US and Thai officials are trying to ensure this happens without any of the salacious headlines for which Pattaya has become known.

The Thai authorities have said there are a few places where the US servicemen and women will not be allowed to go. One of them is Soi 6, which runs down to the main beach, and is known for its concentration of racy go-go bars.

While the Thai police have reminded their US visitors that prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand, there are actually thought to be 25,000 to 50,000 sex workers in the city. Many of them work in Soi 6, where they stand outside the bars imploring men to come inside.
The many cannabis shops in Pattaya are also off-limits to US crew members, along with sea-sports like paragliding and jet-skis.
"It is their decision," Mayor Poramase Ngampiches told the BBC. "The US military have done their homework."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The war in Iran is hurting local businesses

blocks.text: The war in Iran is hurting local businesses
US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson rebuffed questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing.
Instead, he said the US troops would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand".
"We're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can," he said.

The US Navy has organised shuttle buses from the port into Pattaya running from 5am to 2am every day the carrier is here in Thailand. Two hotels have been designated suitable for those US crew members who want to splash out on a night onshore.
The Thai authorities have deployed hundreds of police officers to keep an eye on the city's entertainment zones, and warned local businesses not to overcharge their American guests.
"The visits of US military men 50-60 years ago introduced Pattaya to the world and turned it into a tourist attraction," says Mayor Poramase.
"We have to be frank, the city has a reputation for bar girls. We understand the stereotypes. We can't stop that.
"What we can do is to show that Pattaya has changed, that we now have other things, such as sports, seminars, wellness and family-friendly activities. It's a mixture of everything."
Both countries hope that by the time the USS Abraham Lincoln begins the long journey home across the Pacific on 6 September, it will be with a refreshed and rested crew.
With additional reporting from Nongnapat Patcham.

articles.title: Prosec: Why let Poa talk about secret funds if he’s unaware of ops?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Why did Vice President Sara Duterte pick Michael Poa to answer questions from the Commission on Audit (COA) about P112.5 million in Department of Education (DepEd) confidential…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Why did Vice President Sara Duterte pick Michael Poa to answer questions from the Commission on Audit (COA) about P112.5 million in Department of Education (DepEd) confidential funds if he had no firsthand knowledge of the operations the money was supposedly spent on?

That was one of the points that House private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. tried to clarify as he questioned Poa, former DepEd spokesperson when Duterte still headed the department, who testified on Wednesday as a hostile witness on the 21st day of the vice president’s impeachment trial.
In a statement, the prosecution said it included that issue in a 13-point offer for Poa’s testimony.

Despite being one of the defense lawyers and their legal spokesperson, Poa was presented as a witness, the statement said, for being Duterte’s former DepEd spokesperson, chief of staff, officer-in-charge of finance, and head of the procuring entity. Poa was also the former spokesperson of the Office of the Vice President (OVP).
13-point offer
Following is an overview of the 13-point offer of the prosecution, as described in its statement:
Point 1
This described Poa as “one of the Vice President’s most trusted men,” a relationship the prosecution considers central to his assignment.
Points 2 to 4

These focused on Poa’s knowledge. Tolosa offered to prove that Poa had “no prior participation in the operational use of the confidential funds before COA issued its Audit Observation Memoranda (AOM), yet Duterte directed him to prepare the responses.”

According to the prosecution, the officials Poa consulted could not supply firsthand information either. These were former special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda and then-Undersecretary Nolasco Mempin.

“The documents eventually gathered consisted principally of Armed Forces certifications,” the statement said, referring to the certifications issued by the military on DepEd’s participation in the 2023 Youth Leadership Summits.
Points 5 to 7
These challenged the resulting explanation, with Tolosa alleging that Poa supplied COA with theories and presumptions despite not knowing how the money was spent.

Tolosa said the AFP certifications “did not identify an informer, information purchased, reward paid, or successful operation linked to the payment — the four elements Tolosa used to frame the [COA] Joint Circular requirement.”
According to Tolosa, Poa acknowledged when he said: “There’s no connection at all.”
The prosecution intends to establish that the certifications proved the YLS activities occurred, but did not mention anything about DepEd’s making its alleged reward payments.
Point 8
This focused on Col. Dennis Nolasco, who was then a DepEd security officer.
Tolosa alleged that, following Duterte’s instruction, Fajarda handed the confidential funds to Nolasco. And yet, Nolasco’s name did not appear in Poa’s explanations to COA or during a House hearing.
Point 9
This alleged that Poa and Zuleika Lopez, OVP chief of staff, sought to have COA send an audit query rather than an AOM.
According to the prosecution, this showed the officials’ separate roles to Duterte.
“Different hands carried out the steps. One principal directed them all,” Tolosa argued.
Points 11 and 12
These questioned “the sufficiency of the liquidation despite COA’s issuance of a Credit Notice.”

As Tolosa argued, the notice “rested on military certifications that did not establish the underlying informers, information, or payments, leaving more than ₱15 million in claimed rewards and the broader ₱112.5-million fund without an explained money trail.”
Point 13
The prosecution reserved this for other relevant matters that may come out during Poa’s examination.
‘Rhetoric to provide drama’
“Rhetoric aimed to provide drama in this proceeding,” defense lawyer Sheila Sison said about parts of the offer.
Sison disputed Tolosa’s characterization that Poa answered for ₱112.5 million, saying he replied to audit observations rather than assumed responsibility for the funds.
WATCH: Defense calls prosecution’s 13-point offer on Poa ‘rhetoric’

She also stressed that a COA Credit Notice is an official audit document informing an agency of amounts allowed in audit and rejected the prosecution’s claim that it did not resolve the underlying issue.
Sison took exception to Tolosa’s description of Poa as “ang abogadong walang alam” – a lawyer who knows nothing.
Tolosa explained that he was describing how Poa repeatedly said in the past that he had no personal knowledge of how the confidential funds were used.
But he apologized to Poa, saying: “If I offended you in any way, sir, I’m very sorry for that. That’s not my intention.”
Presiding Officer Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero ordered the phrase stricken, calling it “discourteous.”
He then asked why the prosecution was calling a witness who claimed to lack knowledge,
Tolosa said that was precisely the material issue: Why did Duterte select Poa to answer COA instead of officials who handled or received the money?
After Sison clarified that she had not stipulated to the prosecution’s factual offers, Escudero ruled independently that “the chair will proceed to declare Attorney Poa as a hostile witness.”
That allowed Tolosa to ask leading questions, but, as Escudero reminded him, “ not misleading questions.” /atm

articles.title: Miscommunication prompts troops to stop MILF convoy in Lanao Norte
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY – Miscommunication and lack of coordination prompted government forces to halt a convoy of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) in Kolambugan, Lanao del Norte, Wednesday…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY – Miscommunication and lack of coordination prompted government forces to halt a convoy of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) in Kolambugan, Lanao del Norte, Wednesday morning.

The Lanao del Norte 1st Provincial Mobile Force Company and the Army’s 52nd Mechanized Company under the 5th Mechanized Infantry “Kaagapay” Battalion intercepted the MILF convoy from Picong, Lanao del Sur en route to Camp Bilal in Munai, Lanao del Norte, where they were to attend a meeting.
The MILF convoy was composed of 23 vehicles and five motorcycles, half of them armed with weapons, the military said.
Anwar Alamada, chairman of the MILF Ad Hoc Joint Action Group (AHJAG), clarified that the incident involving members of the MILF was resolved through existing peace mechanisms.

He told the Inquirer that both the Coordinating Committee on the Cessation of Hostilities (CCCH) and the AHJAG worked together to address the incident and ensure compliance with existing ceasefire protocols.
Alamada confirmed that the incident stemmed from miscommunication and a lack of coordination, rather than an intentional violation of the ceasefire agreement.
He said peace mechanisms are in place to address such incidents and prevent their escalation.
The convoy members were safely escorted back, in accordance with CCCH protocols.
Alamada noted that coordination is essential to establish the purpose of travel and determine whether it is related to peacekeeping and other legitimate objectives.
He stressed the need to fully observe ceasefire protocols, including rules governing the carrying of firearms.
Alamada said carrying firearms is discouraged in areas where activities or gatherings are being held, particularly when adequate security measures are already in place.
However, he acknowledged that unintended violations may occur due to lapses or misunderstandings./coa

articles.title: Senate bill banning public officials’ kin from gov’t deals advances
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – A Senate bill prohibiting families of public officials from securing government contracts was approved on third and final reading on Wednesday. Senate Bill No. 1962, or the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A Senate bill prohibiting families of public officials from securing government contracts was approved on third and final reading on Wednesday.

Senate Bill No. 1962, or the “Government Contracting and Procurement Integrity Act,” seeks to disqualify from government procurement and contracts relatives of politicians within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity and affinity.

The measure was authored by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, and Senators. Francis Escudero, Christopher “Bong” Go, Joel Villanueva, Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, JV Ejercito, Loren Legarda and Francis Pangilinan.

SBN 1962 was created “to eliminate potential avenues for corruption and uphold fairness, integrity, transparency, impartiality, and accountability in the procurement process and the utilization of public funds.”

“Relatives of any covered public official or personnel within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity shall be barred from participating in or entering into any government contract or from engaging in subcontracting, consortium, joint venture, or other similar business arrangements for the performance of a government contract,” the measure reads.
The fourth degree of consanguinity and affinity covers the following relatives and their in-law counterparts by marriage or adoption:

items: Parents
Children
Grandparents
Siblings
Grandchildren
Great grandparents
Great aunts and uncles
Great niece and nephews
Great grandchildren
Great great grandparents
Great great aunts and uncles
Great great nieces and nephews
First cousins

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the covered public officials include elected local and national officials, Cabinet secretaries, undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, officers and members of government-owned or -controlled corporations, and state universities and colleges, whether regular or ex officio, as well as their alternates.

Also covered are heads of procuring entities, agents, members of the Bids and Awards Committee (BAC), technical working group, BAC Secretariat, head of property management office, end users or implementing units, or project consultants of any government agency or institution.

Should the bill be passed, violating disqualified entities may be penalized with imprisonment of not less than a year or more than three years and a fine of not less than P100,000 and perpetual disqualification from participating in or entering into government procurement activities.

On the other hand, the public officer engaged in the practice may be held liable for violating graft and corrupt practices, the same imprisonment term and fines, as well as perpetual disqualification from public office. /gsg

articles.title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest
articles.summary:
Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its…

blocks.text: Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.

Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.

The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.

Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.

Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.

blocks.caption: The Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people.  Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/Alamy

blocks.text: Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.

The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.

Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.

The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.

The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.

Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.

“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”

Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.

Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

articles.title: Family pays tribute to New Mexico man killed by bear: ‘He was a strong person’
articles.summary:
Relatives of Benjamin Halona remember his career as wildlife firefighter and his zeal for selling tamales

Relatives of a New…

blocks.text: Relatives of a New Mexico man who was fatally mauled by a bear inside his home recently say they are choosing to remember his firefighting career and zeal for peddling tamales rather than his rare, brutal manner of death.

As Benjamin Halona’s sister, Gloria Halona, and her daughter, Samantha Vandever, put it, that is the least he deserved after the quiet dignity that he showed becoming a widower in February and subsequently grappling with health problems that required him to use a walker and a wheelchair to move around.
“He was a really strong person,” Gloria Halona said of her brother in a telephone interview that her and Vandever granted on Monday. “And, even though he didn’t have a lot, he was happy.”
The pair did not mind sharing new details about the 20 August bear attack that killed Benjamin Halona, 67, as he recovered from a devastating seizure that had drastically limited his mobility.
They said Halona stayed back at his home in the Navajo Nation community of Crystal, New Mexico, while his stepson, Casey, had gone to the post office.
Casey was brought into Halona’s life by his wife, Bernadine, who died six months earlier from illness. He heard Halona lock the front door, according to Gloria and Samantha.
But, when Casey returned home, they said, the door was ajar, and there was a bear inside turning its nose toward him.

Casey instinctively locked himself inside his room; barricaded the door there with a dresser and other heavy items; hid in a crawlspace in his closet; and used a cellphone to dial for emergency help. He also called Gloria and Samantha, who recounted driving over to him and seeing the bear outside the home.

Samantha said she was driving and honked the horn at the bear at her mother’s behest. The bear fled, and a police officer shot the animal, they said. The mother and daughter then went inside the home and encountered a “horrific scene” that made it clear the bear they had seen had just killed Benjamin.

The fact that Benjamin’s walker was inside his room undisturbed made them wonder if he spent his final moments hearing something at the front door and unlocking it mistakenly believing it was his stepson struggling to get inside.
“It was a lot for us,” Samantha said.
A Navajo Nation police department spokesperson on Monday declined to discuss Halona’s death, saying the agency had released what it could in a statement on the day of the bear attack.
That statement said a bear had killed a man in Crystal, had fled into nearby woods, and was killed by police. It also extended condolences to the man’s family.
Regardless, Samantha and Gloria said they had been coping as much as possible by recalling much more pleasant memories of Benjamin.

He sold tamales locally that were a community favorite, they said. They said he was also fiercely proud of having served his Native American reservation as a wildland firefighter – and of the nicknames given to him by his friends and loved ones: Ponjo, Mountain Man and Tamale Man.

Halona’s fandom of the Grammy-winning country singer Waylon Jennings was also a major aspect of his personality, Gloria said. She spoke about how her brother got to share a personal moment with Jennings months before the latter man’s February 2002 death.

Jennings had traveled to Navajo Nation at the time to perform at a fair. Family members managed to arrange a brief meeting, which was photographed and saw Halona and Jennings sing Love of the Common People, which the crooner famously recorded.

“We’re living in the love of the common people, smiles from the heart of a family man,” some that song’s lyrics say. “Daddy’s gonna buy you a dream to cling to, Mama’s gonna love you just as much as she can.”
Jennings complimented Halona by telling him that he sounded better than country legend Willie Nelson, Gloria said. She added: “That was probably the happiest moment of Benjamin’s life.”
Perhaps unsurprisingly, Halona’s fatal bear mauling prompted an intense community reaction.
The Navajo people, for one, regard bears as sacred – and here, they had lost both Halona and a spiritual animal.

There also had evidently not been a deadly bear mauling in New Mexico since 2001, according to a comprehensive list with information about ursine attacks. That 2001 case, furthermore, had been the first fatal New Mexico bear attack in a century, the Associated Press reported.
Nonetheless, eight days before Halona’s death, New Mexico wildlife officials had warned of “an increase in the number of bears involved in human-bear conflict throughout [the state] in 2026”.
They asked the public to avoid leaving garbage and fallen or rotten fruit out, which could draw bears into populated areas amid severe drought conditions that New Mexico was experiencing.

Meanwhile, Gloria and Samantha said his survivors – among them two siblings, four children, five stepchildren, 15 grandchildren and one great-grandchild – were finding support in each other. They said they had also drawn a measure of comfort from the strong attendance at community memorials organized in Halona’s honor as well as at his funeral services on 29 August.
“He endured a lot in his life – especially during his death,” Vandever remarked of her uncle. “And we’re all heartbroken that this had to happen to him.”

articles.title: [Be The Good] Two events next week at the Rappler Civic Hub
articles.summary: This is how we show up for our readers, our partners, and the communities impacted by the stories we cover. We hope you can be part of it.

blocks.text: Hello!
If you’re based in Luzon like me, you’ve likely had to deal with floods, interminable rain, and canceled activities in the past few days.
Here’s to hoping for fair weather ahead, not least because of two events we’re holding at the Rappler Civic Hub on September 10 and September 11.

In these in-person events, we’re putting the spotlight on two public interest issues we’ve been closely following over the past months and weeks: the wealth and properties of former House speaker Martin Romualdez, and the disturbing pattern of school violence.

These are two issues that have to do with accountability, and protecting communities from harms and abuses. While they are distinct topics, they present challenges that need us to work together, instead of in siloes.

The events next week aim to make that happen, or at least light a spark. Both are happening in the Rappler Civic Hub in Estancia Offices in Pasig City. This is the new name we have given our newsroom, because we’ve been using it more and more, not just as an office, but as a space where our community can gather.
Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe? on Thursday, September 10 | 12:30 pm to 5 pm
Here are the two events next week you don’t want to miss:

Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte, Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group spokesperson Police Captain Wallen Arancillo, and child protection expert Dr. Princess Gairanod will headline our pilot Civic Circles. This will combine a high-level panel discussion with a hands-on workshop for key sectors and communities affected by the problem of campus violence. Hear from our panelists about ways they’re dealing with this, then be part of workshops that will connect these to needs on the ground. The goal of Civic Circles is to come up with actionable solutions that will then be amplified by Rappler and our partners. (READ: Psychologists want us to rethink what we ask about school violence)
This event is free, but registration is required ahead of time due to limited space.
From investigation to action: The Romualdez trail, a Rappler+ briefing on Friday, September 11 | 3 pm to 6 pm

We will be livestreaming the panel discussion, so those who can’t make it in-person can contribute to the discussion through the Education chat room on the Rappler app. Download the app for free here.

For our third Rappler+ event this year, our investigative researchers and reporters will bring you inside the multi-part, impact-driven investigation into former House speaker Martin Romualdez’s wealth and properties. It was President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself who announced an upcoming Ombudsman complaint against Romualdez, his own cousin, in relation to public works corruption. It was also Romualdez’s district in Leyte that got the biggest slice of public works funds in the first half of the Marcos presidency.

Amid recantations of Romualdez’ bodyguards affecting the case buildup against him, this special Rappler briefing tells the story from journalists following the Romualdez money trail. Apart from our journalists, we’ve also invited anti-corruption watchdogs to talk about civil society efforts towards holding public officials accountable over the flood control mess. How can we connect the two, and go beyond? Through this much-needed conversation, we want to turn investigation into action.

This event is exclusive to our Rappler+ members. Members who want to confirm attendance just need to check their email inbox for the invitation and confirmation details for this event sent last August 29. Those residing outside Metro Manila can also register to get a Zoom link, through the confirmation details in the email invitation about this event.

If you wish to become a member, you can subscribe for as low as P400 a month here. Members can expect more such events throughout the year. A cheaper Rappler+ Lite subscription gets you access to all Rappler content, but not to the exclusive events. Sign up for Rappler+ membership here.
Rappler+ is how our newsroom stays both independent, and alive. By becoming a member, you directly support our work and protect the integrity of the stories we tell.
Do these two events interest you?
Through activities like these, we hope to widen the reach and impact of our journalism and civic engagement work.
This is how we show up for our readers, our partners, and the communities impacted by the stories we cover. We hope you can be part of it.

articles.title: [In the Public Square] Two months in: Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial so far
articles.summary: The impeachment can be viewed in terms popularized by a late, great constitutionalist: it is 'political justice'

blocks.text: The impeachment can be viewed in terms popularized by a late, great constitutionalist: it is 'political justice'

We’ve just completed Day 21, and Week 9, of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Today, public prosecutor Representative Joel Chua suggested that the prosecution may be able to finish its presentation of evidence in chief by early October. That means, he said, the trial might end by December.
As people say, malayo pa, pero malayo na. Two months in, how goes the impeachment of Sara Duterte?

The impeachment can be viewed in terms popularized by the late, great constitutionalist Fr. Joaquin Bernas SJ: it is “political justice.” It’s important to listen to legal analysts, and we will continue to do so.
But it’s equally important to hear from political scientists, and in this episode of In the Public Square, Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by highly esteemed professors of political science.

Dr. Jean Franco is a professor of political science at the UP Diliman and Arjan Aguirre is assistant professor of political science on leave at the Ateneo de Manila, who is doing his PhD at the University of Pittsburgh.
Catch the episode on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, at 8 pm.-Rappler.com
