articles.title: Plane spotter or Chinese spy? Ontario university student suspected of espionage at airports

image.caption: The FBI said in a criminal complaint that an unidentified man was captured on security video at Chicago O'Hare International Airport on April 21 taking photos of aircraft. The incident was later linked to University of Waterloo student Weiheng Zeng. (U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan

blocks.text: World·New

A University of Waterloo student is suspected of espionage after the FBI said he admitted to accessing airport facilities in Toronto and Chicago, to take photos on behalf of a shadowy figure from China. Weiheng Zeng, himself a Chinese citizen, was arrested in Michigan on Aug. 23 and charged with making false statements.
University of Waterloo student Weiheng Zeng is charged with making false statements in the U.S.
An Ontario university student is suspected of espionage after the FBI said he admitted to accessing airport facilities in Toronto and Chicago to take photos on behalf of a shadowy figure from China.
Weiheng Zeng, himself a Chinese citizen, was arrested in Michigan on Aug. 23 after crossing the Ambassador Bridge from Windsor, Ont. He was charged with one count of making false statements.
Zeng appeared in a federal court in Detroit on Tuesday and agreed to remain in custody as he awaits his trial.

A University of Waterloo undergraduate student born in 2004, Zeng first raised U.S. authorities' suspicions in April, after an incident captured on security video at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport, according to a criminal complaint reviewed by CBC News.

At the time, FedEx employees spotted a man taking photos, climbing a forklift and attempting to open a locked delivery truck and a shipping container in the company's parking lot at the Chicago airport, the criminal complaint said.
According to the complaint, Zeng acknowledged he had climbed the forklift at O'Hare 'to get a better angle to take pictures.'
Investigators later linked Zeng to a dark blue Chrysler Town & Country minivan with Ontario licence plates seen on nearby CCTV.

When he attempted to re-enter the U.S. last month while driving the same vehicle, Zeng told U.S. Customs and Border Protection he was headed to Chicago for a one-day trip. Instead, border officers interviewed him three times.

items: The Canadian suspected of spying on NATO was denied bail. Here's what comes next
Ottawa will look into screening processes amid NATO intern spying allegations

blocks.text: And according to the criminal complaint, his story kept changing.
At first, when border agents found numerous photos of military aircraft on his phone, Zeng purportedly said they were for a flight radar website. He said taking pictures of planes was his hobby.

"Zeng's phone was also found to contain pictures of him and other individuals in tactical clothing and in tactical formations, holding rifle-styled firearms," FBI special agent Robert Holbrook wrote in the complaint. Zeng purportedly said the weapon was an airsoft gun.
He denied having any military service or training.

According to the criminal complaint, Zeng eventually said he was being paid by someone — identified in the U.S. court records only as "Chinese contact" — to photograph specific planes and their tail numbers.

Zeng believed his contact worked for a Chinese security service and that it was "cool," according to documents filed in U.S. District Court in Detroit. Zeng said they had met on a Chinese forum for aviation enthusiasts in 2024.
Chinese SIM cards, Huawei phone
Zeng, who lives in Cambridge, Ont., also outlined to investigators a convoluted system he purportedly used to communicate with the unnamed individual, who paid him via bank transfer in Chinese yuan.
The "Chinese contact" would mail Zeng a new SIM card every four to five months, which he was directed to use in his Huawei cell phone, according to the criminal complaint.
"Zeng, at the direction of 'Chinese Contact,' would subsequently destroy the SIM cards, delete the conversations, and delete the photos he took," wrote Holbrook, the FBI agent.
"The SIM card, which was from China Telecom, allowed Zeng to by-pass Canadian cellular network and connect directly with the Chinese provider network to send text messages to 'Chinese Contact.' "
In a separate interview last month with the FBI, Zeng purportedly said his contact had directed him in October 2025 to take photos inside a FedEx facility at Toronto Pearson International Airport.
He said he was confronted by a FedEx employee and only managed to take pictures outside the building. Still, he said he sent the photos to his contact and received the equivalent of $200 US.
Zeng a flight risk, prosecutor says
At Zeng's first court appearance in Detroit last week, a federal prosecutor said he posed a flight risk and urged that Zeng be held in custody.
"He is a foreign resident and a foreign citizen," assistant U.S. attorney Alyse Wu told the court.

items: Court decision barring Chinese student sends message about espionage risk, experts say

blocks.text: "According to what is alleged in the complaint, his only known tie to this district appears to be using it as a crossing point to enter our country for what appears to be espionage-type activities."

At another hearing on Tuesday, a court-appointed federal defender said Zeng consented to remain in custody. Speaking through a Mandarin-language interpreter, Zeng confirmed his name and his understanding that he would remain behind bars.
The allegations against him have not been proven in court.
It's unclear what undergraduate program Zeng was enrolled in, or when he first came to Canada.
University of Waterloo spokesperson Pamela Smyth told CBC News in an email, "we don't normally comment on ongoing criminal matters."

items: 4 ex-Western University students accused in London, Ont., explosives-making scheme face 19 new charges

blocks.text: Waterloo police said they weren't involved in the investigation.
The Chinese embassies in Ottawa and Washington did not respond to requests for comment.
If you have a news tip related to this story, contact CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle by email: thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Indonesian wildfire haze degrades Northern Mindanao air quality
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — Transboundary smoke drifting from raging forest and land fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, has triggered deteriorating air quality across Northern Mindanao, sending pollution…

blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — Transboundary smoke drifting from raging forest and land fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, has triggered deteriorating air quality across Northern Mindanao, sending pollution gauges in neighboring Iligan City to “acutely unhealthy” levels.

Air monitoring data released by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Environmental Management Bureau-10 (DENR-EMB-10) revealed a steady spike in fine particulate matter between August 30 and September 1 across key urban centers.
Iligan City recorded the most alarming spike, with its Air Quality Index (AQI) surging past the 200 threshold into the acutely unhealthy range — registering 203 on Aug. 31 and 209 on Sept. 1.
In Cagayan de Oro City, conditions deteriorated from “fair” (78 on Aug. 30 and 96 on Aug. 31) to “Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups” on Sept. 1 after posting an AQI of 105.

Nearby Tagoloan town remained lodged in the “Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups” bracket throughout the three days, recording consecutive readings of 109 on Aug. 30 and 31 before climbing to 140 on Sept. 1.

Nick Jabagat, chief of this city’s Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Department, said they had just met with the City Health Office and the City Local Environment and Natural Resources Office (CLENRO) to discuss the air quality.

“If you have to go out, wear a face mask and please monitor the updates on the official Facebook pages of CHO and CLENRO, which are posting the current air quality in the city,” Jabagat told the Inquirer on Wednesday.

Under EMB guidelines, an AQI between 201 and 300 warns that people should avoid heavy traffic corridors, people with heart or respiratory conditions like asthma must stay indoors and rest, and unnecessary travel should be postponed.
DENR-EMB-10 attributed the regional haze to prevailing wind currents funneling transboundary smoke and particulate matter across borders.
“The haze observed in some areas of the Philippines is associated with transboundary smoke from forest and land fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia,” the bureau said in an advisory./coa

articles.title: The battle that made Canada bleed: Operation Medusa, 20 years later
articles.summary: It has been 20 years since Canadian soldiers walked into a Taliban killing ground west of Kandahar. Operation Medusa became Canada’s largest battle since Korea — a brutal test against a disciplined,…

image.caption: A Canadian soldier calls in an airstrike Saturday, Sept. 2, 2006, the first day of Operation Medusa in Kandahar, Afghanistan. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: As Canadian troops crossed the Arghandab River, the first indication to former corporal Bruce Moncur that something was amiss came with the sight of a green pen flare shooting across the sky.
"I remember looking at it thinking, well, that's weird," said Moncur, who realized that since NATO troops in Afghanistan fired red flares, green must have belonged to the Taliban.
"That was an indication that we had walked far enough into the trap."
The Taliban had waited until he and his section of troops had dismounted from the protection of their armoured vehicles before springing their three-sided ambush.
Moncur recalls every detail of that day 20 years ago with a stark, blinding clarity.
It was the opening phase of Operation Medusa, a savage, close-quarters battle in the vineyards and dusty villages of Kandahar.
'I'll never forget': Canadian veteran recalls opening phases of Operation Medusa
The battle began on Sept. 2, 2006, with an artillery and air bombardment.
A day later, Moncur's unit set off to cross the river.
The Canadians ran into a deeply entrenched enemy that was firing machine guns, rocket-propelled grenades and small arms.
The battle was different in the sense the Taliban force had chosen, unusually, to stand and fight.
More than 2,000 NATO troops, including over 1,000 Canadians, took part, alongside Afghan forces and American, British, Dutch and Danish elements.
It would be the biggest battle Canadians had fought since Korea and their largest conventional operation of the Afghan war.
Canadian veterans on the legacy of Afghanistan war

Moncur's unit, Charles Company, 1st Battalion Royal Canadian Regiment (1RCR), had been drawn into the insurgent ambush after crossing the river as they were pushing toward their objective, a little white school house the Taliban had occupied.

The firefight lasted five hours. Four Canadian soldiers were killed: Warrant Officer Frank Mellish, Warrant Officer Richard Nolan, Sgt. Shane Stachnik and Pte. William Cushley. An additional 16 troops were wounded before the order was given to retreat.

"In that firefight, I was all over the battlefield. Some vehicles were stuck and left behind, and we had to try to salvage them," Moncur said. "One soldier was left behind. We obviously don't leave anyone behind. So, we had to go and rescue his body."

In an interview given to reporters at the time, the commander of Bravo Company 1 RCR said the depth and strength of the Taliban force, which were later estimated at a total of 1,000 insurgents, was not something the Canadians expected.

items: Rebalancing or retreat? Canada's peacekeeping legacy fades away
5 years after Taliban seized control, Afghan refugee reflects on new life in Saskatoon

blocks.text: "Truthfully, I was surprised by the resistance they put up," the commander, Maj. Geoff Abthorpe, said. "We came at them with what I perceived to be a pretty heavy fist."
"I think closer to about 400 Taliban fighters and men that had fought all their lives versus 80 Canadians that had … this is their first time at combat, first time in a real firefight," said Moncur.
In the late summer of 2006 prior to the battle, hundreds of insurgents had massed in the Panjwai and Zhari districts, roughly 30 kilometres west of Kandahar city, the provincial capital.
They had dug trenches, fortified compounds, planted mines and improvised explosive devices and established defensive positions around the nearby village of Pashmul.

The timing was deliberate. NATO had only recently taken responsibility for southern Afghanistan from the U.S.-led coalition, and the Taliban appeared determined to test whether the alliance had the stomach for a serious fight.
Sean Maloney, a historian at the Royal Military College of Canada, said all throughout the spring and summer of 2006 Canadian troops had been fighting running battles with the Taliban.
The ones that decided to fight in Pashmul were different. They were better trained, more co-ordinated and better equipped.

There has been a long running debate in Canadian and U.S. military circles about whether Pakistan's notorious intelligence service had contributed — in some way — to the sophistication of the insurgents who fought NATO forces.
"They're definitely a major factor in this," said Maloney.

A U.S. military study of insurgent tactics, written long after the battle in 2018, also pointed to potential Pakistani involvement, including the redirection of foreign fighters to bolster the ranks of local Taliban.
The report noted how the insurgents mounted planned ambushes and counterattacks and, when NATO firepower became overwhelming, conducted what the study calls a "disciplined retreat."

Several weeks after the operation, Pakistani journalist and noted Taliban expert Ahmed Rashid wrote a piece quoting NATO commanders, who believed the battle had exposed the Taliban’s support structure in Pakistan to an "extraordinary degree."
Friendly fire
After the failed river crossing on the second day of the battle, disaster struck Moncur's unit again.
An American A-10 mistakenly strafed Canadian positions, killing Pte. Mark Graham and wounding more than 30 others, including Moncur, who suffered a major head injury.

"I'm sitting there eating, and my fire team partner comes to sit next to me,' said Moncur, who compared the sensation of being strafed to being electrocuted. "I just remember being tossed in the air like a rag doll…. I remember feeling like my body was being, like I touched a socket or something."
He tumbled down a rocky slope before losing consciousness. When Moncur came to, he knew his head was bleeding.
"If you've ever washed your face in a basin and just filled up and splashed yourself with water, that's how much blood ended up filling in my hands," Moncur said.
He crawled to a nearby medic, who was also wounded, before passing out again.

items: Canada's top soldier expresses pride in 'who we are,' after Hegseth targets cadets in post
Five years after Kabul fell, the reckoning over Afghanistan is far from over

blocks.text: "I basically made peace with this. That was going to be the final moments of my life," Moncur said.
But it wasn't.
He was rushed to the military hospital at Kandahar Airfield before being evacuated to a U.S. military trauma centre in Germany, where he faced a long, painful road to recovery.
Following the friendly fire attack, Charles Company was effectively removed from the battle.
Canadian Afghan war veteran describes being wounded by friendly fire
The commanders — Brig.-Gen. David Fraser and Lt.-Col. Omer Lavoie — shifted the axis of the main attack to the north.
The battered remnants of Charles Company remained in the south, helping convince the Taliban another river assault was coming, while Canadian forces pushed down from Highway 1.
The operation lasted another two weeks and ended with hundreds of insurgents killed.
Maloney said it was a pivotal moment in the war. The intention of the Taliban, at the time, was to eventually push into Kandahar city.
The decisive defeat forced them to switch back to hit-and-run tactics of improvised explosives and ambushes.
It was also an important political moment.
"That's when the Afghans realized, yeah, we're going to fight," Maloney said. "And as one of them walked up to our people and said — in shock — you're willing to bleed for us."

articles.title: The U.S. could control 20% of Venezuela's oil reserves. Canada's oilpatch isn't worried
articles.summary: U.S President Donald Trump is continuing his pursuit of Venezuela's oil jackpot, announcing a new deal aimed at boosting production in the South American country. And while Trump is flaunting the…

image.caption: A macaw stands on a decorative oil drill in Caracas, Venezuela. U.S. President Donald Trump is flaunting the potential controlling stake in a portion of Venezuela's oil reserves as a warning to Canada. (Matias Delacroix/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: U.S. President Donald Trump is continuing his pursuit of Venezuela's oil jackpot, announcing a new deal aimed at boosting production in the South American country. And while Trump is flaunting the potential controlling stake in a portion of Venezuela's oil reserves as a warning to Canada, experts say there is little cause for concern in Western Canada.
An increase in Venezuelan exports to refineries located on the U.S. Gulf Coast would pose a competitive threat to the Alberta oilpatch, since both produce a similar type of heavy oil.

Venezuela boasts some of the largest underground deposits of oil, yet the country faces a number of challenges to ramping up production, in addition to political instability that could sink any ambition to rejuvenate the country’s oilpatch.

At the same time, the Canadian oilpatch is continuing to set new records for production, in addition to a handful of new and expansion pipeline projects in various stages of development to boost export volumes. Despite the ongoing trade war, the U.S. continues to increase its use of Canadian oil — which last year accounted for more than 60 per cent of the country's crude oil imports.

A noticeable ramp-up of Venezuelan oil exports is still five to 10 years away, experts say, which is why the possible threat to Canada is not an urgent problem, said Ed Sprague, a former deputy energy minister in Alberta.
"If the Americans want to pursue this, they are going to have to spend time and [an] awful lot of money," said Sprague, about the deal struck between the U.S. and Venezuela.
"One of the things we know about it is we don’t know very much about it," he said.
The new 'deal'

On Friday, Trump announced on social media that his administration had struck a deal with Venezuela to obtain majority control of one-fifth of the country’s oil reserves. As part of the agreement, the U.S. will have a direct equity stake in a private company, led by a Venezuelan businessman.

Trump described the arrangement as greatly increasing the U.S.'s oil supply and securing majority control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves. Meanwhile, Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodríguez said the deal will bring in tens of billions of dollars in investment, while maintaining the country's "ownership of and sovereignty" over its natural resources.
Trump announces Venezuela oil reserves will be controlled by U.S.
Those two messages are "quite a bit different," said Al Salazar, a Calgary-based analyst with Enverus, an energy analytics company.
"There’s a bit of discrepancy about what’s going on. It does give you pause," he said. "Nobody knows what the terms are yet."

That's part of the reason why Canadian oil executives are taking note of the deal, but won’t be losing sleep over it. Instead, they’ll wait for any actual progress in reviving the depleted Venezuelan industry.
"Show me the barrel first before anyone actually moves," he said of the reaction in the Canadian industry.

The Trump administration has been pressuring American oil and gas executives to invest in Venezuela's energy sector, after the U.S. military attacked the country, capturing then-president Nicolás Maduro in January.
Oilsands decades ahead

The majority of Canada's heavy oil comes from the oilsands region in Northern Alberta, where mines and industrial sites produce millions of barrels every day and have become one of the lowest cost sources of oil in North America.

One of the big advantages of the oilsands is that the multi-billion dollar facilities are all built, paid-off and continuously are improved, said Alex Filstein, a technology developer and reservoir engineer in the oilsands.

"We don’t need to spend more money on facilities. We just manufacture that oil. We just run those facilities. We have political stability and we have a very low cost of supply in Canada," said Filstein, who is the chief technology officer at Watercut Inc.
It's a stark contrast to Venezuela, which, at its peak in 1970, produced 3.7 million barrels per day.
The country only pumped about 900,000 barrels per day out of the ground last year, following many years of declining investment because of sanctions and failed government policies.

Not only is the oil industry infrastructure in various states of disrepair and neglect, experts say its unknown how much money will be required to make those repairs, let alone construct new infrastructure.

"Nobody really knows the integrity of these facilities," said Filstein, who describes the vague details and uncertainty in Venezuela as a major impediment for major US energy companies who may be reluctant to invest in Venezuela. The companies may choose to instead invest the dollars in their other operations around the world.
"Companies need stability and they need to know exactly how the dollars are allocated," said Filstein.
Albertans excited and cautious about Venezuelan oil opportunities
Political hurdles
Besides the practical challenges, there is political instability, too.
If Venezuela's oil industry does indeed rebound, by the time that happens, both the U.S. and Venezuela will likely have different leaders and potentially new governments as well.

"There is an open question about when Venezuela returns to democracy, would a future government honour this deal? So for the companies looking to invest, there's significant cost risk as well as significant political risk in doing so,” said Colin Mang, an economics professor at McMaster University in Hamilton.
"It's not clear that American oil companies will invest, at least not to the extent that the Trump administration is hoping," he said.
In past decades, foreign companies have had their Venezuelan assets seized. In the case of ExxonMobil, it happened twice.

items: Trump says U.S. makes deal to control 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves

blocks.text: So far, a handful of companies, including Shell and Repsol, have expressed interest in potential new investments in Venezuela's oil and gas industry. Chevron, which already has operations in the country, is considering an expansion.
The prospect of more heavy oil imports into the U.S. is not something Canada should be fearful of, said Sprague, the former Alberta deputy energy minister.
He points to how demand for oil around the world continues to climb and Canada is increasing its exports off the West Coast to foreign markets including China and India.
The Trans Mountain pipeline system, which transports oil from Edmonton to the Vancouver area, is at capacity, and an initial expansion is expected to be completed by the end of the year.

The Alberta government is also partnering with the federal government to develop a new pipeline project along a similar route. The federal government is expected to decide by Oct. 1, whether to designate the proposal as a "project of national interest" under the Building Canada Act.
"The United States is looking for a diversity of sources. That's OK. We're thinking of a diversity of markets,” said Sprague.

articles.title: Lululemon the latest brand to bet on resale as second-hand clothing becomes big business
articles.summary: Shoppers looking to save money on Lululemon apparel have another option. The athletic wear company has launched its resale site in Canada. A 25,000 square foot processing hub in Calgary is at the…

image.caption: Peter Whitcomb, CEO of Tersus Solutions, a Denver-based company that has opened its first facility in Canada to process resale items for Lululemon. Whitcomb said the company's business in the U.S. has grown tenfold in the past five years, as more brands look for ways to recover value from returned a

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Shoppers looking to save money on Lululemon apparel have another option. The athletic wear company has launched its resale site in Canada. A 25,000 square foot processing hub in Calgary is at the center of the expansion.
Launch of clothing brand's Like New platform is the latest sign retailers see growing opportunity in resale
Lululemon is the latest retailer to expand into the resale market, as second-hand shopping increasingly moves from thrift stores and online marketplaces into brands' own ecosystems.
The Vancouver-based athletic and leisurewear company joins other major brands like Canada Goose and Arc'teryx that are rethinking their approach to used clothing.

The effects of that rethink can be seen inside a 25,000-square-foot processing hub in Calgary run by Tersus Solutions, where Lululemon returns are being cleaned, graded and processed for resale as part of the brand's Like New service.
It's the first Canadian facility opened by Denver-based Tersus, which, along with returns, will also handle used Lululemon items sold for resale by customers across the country.

items: Lululemon's net income down as brand promises product shakeup

blocks.text: Experts say the appeal of resale to companies is simple: a product that might otherwise be written off can potentially be sold again, while they can earn loyalty from buyers, who are reimbursed with credit that can go toward other products.
That means customers benefit by saving on newer products, while there also an obvious benefit in terms of sustainability.
Lululemon launched Like New in Canada last month. Customers can buy and sell their pre-owned Lululemon clothing with other customers through the online platform.
According to its FAQ page, customers can receive 70 per cent of the sale price in cash or 90 per cent in store credit.
To sell an item, listers need a receipt for proof of purchase — but some items might be eligible for a trade in if there's no receipt, according to the Like New website.
Lululemon declined an interview.

"Our products are created with high standards for technical performance and quality, which makes them perfectly suited for life well beyond a single owner," said Maureen Erickson, Lululemon's senior vice-president of retail experience, in a news release.
"Like New extends the life of that product, giving guests a trusted way to keep great gear in use."
'One of their higher margin business lines'
At Tersus Solutions' Calgary facility, clothing is inspected then cleaned using a proprietary liquid CO2 cleaning system that doesn't require any water. They're then refurbished and graded.

Even though the facility is mostly focusing on returned items for resale at this stage, the number of orders it's processing has been "phenomenal" so far, according to Tersus general manager Steve Bommer, who says the facility has been receiving between 1,000 and 1,500 items a day.
While the majority of items being processed for now are in-store or online returns, the numbers are "far exceeding" expectations, Bommer said.

items: Copycats are frustrating but hard to stop in fashion business: experts

blocks.text: Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb said the company's business in the U.S. has grown tenfold in the past five years, as more brands look for ways to recover value from returned and used merchandise.

"If you talk to any of our customers, they would actually say this is one of their higher margin business lines because these are damaged goods that are getting written off and they're getting sold again," said Whitcomb.
He added that Tersus works with brands including New Balance, The North Face and Arc'teryx in the U.S. and is planning to expand in Canada.

David Ian Gray, a retail analyst with DIG360 Consulting and instructor in retails studies at Capilano University in North Vancouver, B.C., said retailers are looking for ways to tap into a second-hand market where their products are already bought and sold.
"The use of Facebook Marketplace, in particular, has just exploded for pre-owned items and the buying and selling of pre-owned items has certainly gone mainstream in Canada," said Gray.
A DIG360/Angus Reid Institute study released in August 2025 found 77 per cent of Canadians bought pre-owned items in the past year.
For retailers, Gray said bringing resale under their own brand can open the door to customers who may not be willing or able to pay full price for their products.

"They could be drawing in some new customers and they could be bringing different price points and different quality levels to people that maybe economically, especially right now are under some pressure to manage budgets."

items: Former Nike executive to take over as Lululemon's new CEO

blocks.text: Outside a Calgary Lululemon, shopper Stacey Hannah said she already looks for a deal and would consider buying or selling through the company's resale platform.
"With the economy the way it is, sometimes you can't spend the money on things. I usually shop the sale rack. [The resale platform] would definitely be something that I would use," Hannah said.
Early adopters of resale
Victoria-based clothing company Anián was an early adopter of resale, launching its own marketplace for customers to sell their Anián products to other shoppers in 2021.
"Circularity is built into the principals of Anián from the beginning. We start with post-consumer recycled fabrics," said COO Jeff Papa.
Papa said the resale site has attracted about 250,000 visits over the past two years and generated roughly $200,000 worth of sales.
"That also represents about 3,600 pounds [1,630 kilograms] of textile waste that we've kept out of the landfill through that program," he said.
Sellers receive the full sale price as credit toward another Anián purchase.
"It's an easy entry into the brand at price points that are 40 per cent of what our retail value is," said Papa.
Other companies have been doing this even longer.
IKEA Canada launched its Sell-back program in 2019. The company said in the 2025 fiscal year, 12,371 items were brought back through the program, with customers receiving an in-store credit.
Gray said offering resale doesn't necessarily mean turning a premium brand into a discount retailer.
"It's not a discount model. It's a model that works at a different price point," he said.

articles.title: Neskantaga First Nation's lack of health-care infrastructure forces evacuation of dozens to Toronto
articles.summary: Four weeks after Neskantaga First Nations declared a state of emergency over a sewage spill at its nursing station, a fire at the temporary health-care facility has left the community scrambling…

image.caption: A sewage spill prompted a Neskantaga First Nation state of emergency in northwestern Ontario after an Aug. 4 sewage spill led to the shutdown of the nursing station, shown in this Thursday photo. (Neskantaga First Nation/Facebook)

blocks.text: Thunder Bay·New

Four weeks after Neskantaga First Nations declared a state of emergency over a sewage spill at its nursing station, a fire at the temporary health-care facility has left the community scrambling again. Officials with Indigenous Services Canada have visited the First Nation to assess the situation, which has forced the relocation of about 250 vulnerable people to Toronto.
Fire disrupts interim health-care facility, ISC officials visit First Nation to assess things

More than four weeks after Neskantaga First Nations declared a state of emergency (SOE) over a sewage spill at its nursing station, a fire at its temporary health-care facility has left the community scrambling again.

The sewage spill in the remote Ojibway community, about 440 kilometres northeast of Thunder Bay, Ont., happened five days after more than 140 community members had returned home from Toronto following an evacuation triggered by nearby wildfires.
Fewer than 400 people live in the First Nation, with about 250 of the community’s most vulnerable now staying in Toronto because of the sewage spill.
Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) officials, including the department’s Ontario regional director general, visited the First Nation on Thursday to assess the situation.

In a statement on Friday, Neskantaga Chief Gary Quisses said he and the ISC officials saw “all the ways the past remediation work done on the nursing station was not done up to code.” That included a 15-cm (six-inch) open gap left in the exterior wall leading into the crawlspace, and black mould that was caused by raw sewage flooding and was spreading in the basement.
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy-Gull Masty has been in contact with Quisses about his concerns, according to an ISC spokesperson.

“ISC is working closely with the Nation to identify and implement additional interim health service solutions while the assessment of the main facility is underway,” Maryéva Métellus said in an email to CBC News on Tuesday.
Discussions “have focused on ensuring support is tailored to the community's evolving needs.”

“In addition to available funding, ISC is prepared to provide practical assistance across a range of areas, from planning and co-ordination to on-the-ground support,” Métellus added. “Conversations with the Nation are ongoing, and ISC is committed to taking timely action to help address urgent needs as they are identified.”
‘We don't want a feasibility study’

Neskantaga’s Child and Family Resources Centre has been used as a temporary nursing station since the sewage spill. Shortly after ISC’s visit, Quisses said, a space heater caused a small fire in the facility.

While the building is still being used, Quisses said it’s not rated for medical equipment. The First Nation is weighing its options for another temporary health clinic, which may mean either using its administrative office, connecting services to a few modular buildings in the community or repurposing trailers at the school.
“What I want my community to have is a functional clinic in the community that will accommodate us so we could repatriate our membership,” Quisses told CBC News on Tuesday.

This isn’t the first time the nursing station has prompted an evacuation; last year, the community’s most vulnerable were evacuated for three months over a flood and smell of fuel at the facility, which was built in 1994.
At the same time, Neskantaga remains under Canada's longest-ever boil-water advisory, which has been in place for 31 years.

items: Amid 2nd evacuation this summer, Neskantaga First Nation calls on Ontario, feds to act
Sewage leak forces another evacuation of Neskantaga First Nation

blocks.text: While there's no timeline for the permanent nursing station to reopen, Quisses said he continues to advocate for a new facility to be built.

“We don't want a feasibility study. We want one step up ahead, the pre-design stage, so that's what we're asking for,” he said. “It will take a few years, I guess, if we're going to get approved for a new clinic.”

When asked about the community’s desires for a new nursing station, Métellus said “we continue to work with the Nation on both its immediate response needs and discuss its longer-term health infrastructure priorities, including the Nation’s request for a new health facility.
“Discussions remain ongoing at this time."
Matawa chiefs want working group created
Neskantaga is part of the Matawa First Nations Management tribal council, which represents eight First Nations in Treaty 9 and one in the Robinson-Superior area.
Matawa issued a statement last week, calling Neskantaga's SOE “the result of failure of the Crowns of Canada and Ontario.”

“The unequal terms of James Bay Treaty No. 9 (1905-06 and 1929-30) leaves our remote First Nations to have to continuously address critical community infrastructure breakdowns, and funding tied to the approval of the government of the day,” the statement says.

The Matawa chiefs are calling on Gull-Masty to respond to Neskantaga’s request for a new nursing station, and for both the provincial and federal governments to “appoint a specifically mandated working group until the state of emergency is lifted by the First Nation.”

items: Neskantaga First Nation calls on province to communicate better amid wildfire emergency
Wildfire evacuees from First Nations in northern Ontario face stressors beyond being far from home

blocks.text: Quisses said his members are growing restless in Toronto. The evacuation disrupted the First Nation's summer festival and youth retreat in August, and with the new school year looming, he's concerned about what will happen to students who have been displaced.
Quisses said he's doing what he can to address the loneliness and isolation faced by evacuees.
“It’s getting to that point where social issues start to arise.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sarah Law is a CBC News reporter based in Thunder Bay, Ont., and has also worked for newspapers and online publications elsewhere in the province. Have a story tip? You can reach her at sarah.law@cbc.ca.

articles.title: EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
articles.summary: The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the attempted attack had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." She said the EU was summoning a Russian envoy, with France announcing a…

image.caption: Kallas and other EU foreign ministers are in Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU presidencyImage: Ansgar Haase/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Unions's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that she summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels over the alleged attempted hybrid attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.

Germany's foreign and interior ministers said in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the government in Berlin had concluded that Russia was responsible for the failed attack, reinforcing suspicions that arose as soon as the news broke in August.
Kallas says incident has 'all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism'

"We are discussing the Leipzig attacks, and also it is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," Kallas said ahead of an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.
"The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador," she said.

The former Estonian prime minister also said that the EU was continuing its work on its next package of some 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's war in Ukraine and said "maybe there is more to be added."
France takes similar step, summoning charge d'affaires
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also told reporters in Dublin that Paris was summoning a Russian ambassador in response.
"I have summoned the Russian charge d'affaires in Paris to protest, Barrot said, adding that sanctions should be taken at a European level, notably against Russia's so-called shadow fleet of ships.
What has Germany said about its investigations?

Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the federal government in Berlin held Russia responsible for the failed attack.

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," Dobrindt said on Tuesday, without going into specifics.
Wadephul said that the "means used — drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine."
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig
Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, have rejected the allegations and accused Germany of fabricating its version of events.

Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key freight hub. Ukrainian airline and aircraft manufacturer Antonov uses the airport as a base of operations, frequently transiting material to Ukraine via the the eastern German city.

articles.title: What really helps Europe deal with drought
articles.summary: Fix leaks or ban pools: As European countries prepare for hotter, drier years to come, here's what the data says about how to really save water

image.caption: Image: Ina Fassbender/AFP

blocks.text: Europe is in drought. As the burning of fossil fuels pushes up temperatures that are making summers hotter and drier, the continent's soils, lakes and rivers are struggling to recover. Southern and Western European countries are particularly affected. But they're not the only ones.

"We've seen drought risks expanding northward during the last decade", says Gisela Elsner, Climate and Sustainability Policy Officer at the German Konrad Adenauer Foundation, who has followed EU water management efforts for years.
"Central and Western Europe, but also southeastern European countries, are increasingly vulnerable due to climate change."
For the month of August this year, satellite data shows areas as far north as Denmark and Sweden experiencing extremely dry conditions more often seen in regions such as the Sub-Saharan Sahel.

The impact is palpable. Some of the continent's longest rivers like the Rhine or the Danube have reached historic lows, disrupting inland shipping routes. Farmers from Germany to Ukraine are reporting below-average harvests, and areas from the United Kingdom to Switzerland to Germany have announced restrictions on household water use.
German municipalities impose water restrictions

To make matters worse, this year's El Niño event — a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures — is set to be one of the strongest on record. Experts predict that 2027 will be even hotter and drier as a result.
Europe will have to adapt to this reality, says Gisela Elsner. "It is not yet a matter of not having water in our taps anymore. But we need to prioritize and use our water resources efficiently."
So, how can countries across the continent set about doing this? DW analyzed water usage in European nations and reviewed the evidence to find out which measures have the most impact.
Which European countries use the most water?

Private households in Europe account for a relatively small share of water usage. Depending on the country, they consume a daily per capita average of between 50 and 300 liters, which equates to less than 20% of all use.
Two thirds of water withdrawn continent-wide is for agriculture — mostly for irrigation — as well as electricity cooling for nuclear and fossil fuel power plants.
In already drought-prone countries like Greece, Turkey and Spain, agriculture accounts for most of the near 2000 liters of water withdrawn per person each day.

Electricity cooling is the biggest factor in Eastern European countries like Bulgaria or Hungary, but also in the Netherlands or Estonia, which use between 1000 and 2000 liters per capita daily in total.
Where Europe can save the most water
"There is no single solution that is sufficient to solve this challenge," says Gisela Elsner. "It has to be a combined bundle of measures."
And they exist. A recent report published by the European Environmental Agency (EEA) found that EU countries could save between 10 and 40% of water annually by implementing targeted strategies.

For states in Western and Eastern Europe, shifting to clean energy would make a big difference. While nuclear, and planet-heating oil, gas and coal need huge amounts of water for cooling, wind and solar do not.
Electricity cooling: renewables to the rescue

So besides becoming the cheapest forms of energy, the renewables that are increasingly replacing fossil fuels are also helping countries to save water. Over the past two decades, Europe has reduced its water usage by around a quarter — mostly because of more efficient electrical cooling.

Even with nuclear plants still requiring water in countries like France, Spain or Sweden, the potential savings are massive. The EEA estimates that EU countries could make significant further savings of between 45 and 95% — equal to hundreds of liters per person each day — by expanding renewables and improving cooling systems.
Better irrigation can help in agriculture

In Southern Europe, agriculture is the big-ticket item. The EEA report recommends, for instance, replacing open water transport channels with closed pipes to avoid evaporation during heatwaves, switching from surface irrigation to sprinklers or drip irrigation, and opting for less water-intensive crops whereever possible.
Public water supply: leaky pipes lose lots of water

In EU countries, around one in four liters of drinkable water from the public supply is lost to leaky pipes and evaporation before it ever reaches its destination — according to estimates by the European association of water providers EurEau.
In Romania and Italy, the share is more than 40%. According to the EEA report, avoiding these losses would account for most of the potential savings in the EU's public water supply.

Once drinking water reaches households and businesses, individual behavior has an impact as well. The EEA report lists extensive recommendations for savings in daily life, from low-flow toilets and efficient washing machines and dishwashers, to harvesting rainwater. Yet even if every citizen in Europe did all they could, it would only reduce the daily per person household water use by between 10 and 40%.

Citizens could also contribute through more responsible consumer decisions, such as considering the water footprint of the products they buy or support, says Alexander Psomas, water resources expert at the Greek consultancy Brilliant Solutions, who co-authored the EEA report.
"Citizens can also push our governments to be more accountable on their energy policy and the impact it has on water."
What Europe can learn

Drought and heat waves are not just a European problem. Many parts in the world are even more severely affected by the climate crisis. And data from the United Nations shows regions in Northern Africa, the Middle East and Asia have been dealing with much higher levels of water stress for a long time.

This also means that Europe can collaborate with, and learn from, the rest of the world on how to adapt to water scarcity. "The UN World Food Program and the FAO are all working on similar questions in the Global South," said Giriraj Armanath, Research Group Leader at the International Water Management Institute.
What one of the world's driest cities teaches us about water
Gisela Elsner recounts, for instance, chip manufacturers in the German state of Saxony recently looking to expertise from Singapore on how to reuse wastewater to cool their factories.
"We can definitely learn from those countries which already have all the knowledge and the technologies that can be used in our context as well," she said.
Public and politics are paying more attention to water use
Both Gisela Elsner and Alexander Psomas say they have noticed both politics and the public becoming more aware in recent years.

"The water scarcity and droughts topic did not have a relevant EU working group until 2022", Psomas told DW. "Today, it's one of the working groups with the highest participation. There is a growing interest and concern on this issue."
What he would like to see more of, he says, is public debates about water strategies, especially during election periods.

"If a country runs low on water, it affects everyone," he says. "I would like to see politicians discuss what kind of solutions they're offering for making their countries more water resilient in 10, 20 years from now."
Edited by Tamsin Walker and Gianna Grün
All

articles.title: Andy Burnham to face first PMQs as borrowing costs rise – UK politics live
articles.summary:
PMQs comes as Resolution Foundation says it is not ‘realistic’ to think defence spending can increase without tax rises

Good morning. Andy Burnham will face PMQs for the…

blocks.text: Good morning. Andy Burnham will face PMQs for the first time as PM today but he already has a fairly good idea of the questions he might get from Kemi Badenoch because she rehearsed them all yesterday. Here is an excerpt from the press release the Conservatives put out yesterday summarising those questions – and their take on how Burnham responded.

double quotation markKemi Badenoch asked if Burnham would: -Set out a plan to get defence spending to 3% of GDP; -Confirm whether Labour will use a Rwanda-style deal to secure our borders; -Set out a timeline to get foreign-born prisoners out of British prisons; -Pledge no new taxes at the forthcoming budget; and -Stand up to his own backbenchers and cut benefits. In response, Burnham floundered and couldn’t give straight answers to clear, straight questions.
Today Badenoch may well ask again about tax, benefit cuts and the economy.

And that is because, while Westminster was focused on Burnham’s impressive debut in the Commons yesterday afternoon, the more significant story may have been happening elsewhere, on the financial markets. The Telegraph sums it up like this.

blocks.caption: Telegraph splash Photograph: Telegraph

blocks.text: Not for the first time, the Telegraph’s headline was not entirely fair to a Labour prime minister. As Heather Stewart explains in her Guardian story, the government’s long-term borrowing costs did jump “to their highest level since early 1998 on Tuesday as investors dumped government bonds” – but this was mainly the result of international factors.

As Graeme Wearden reports in his business live blog today, the UK is not the only country where government borrowing costs are soaring; Graeme says Australia, India and Germany are among other states facing similar problems.

But, just because the UK is not alone, that does not mean the problem is not real; as Heather reports in her story, the rise in borrowing costs means the Treasury has lost £12bn from its fiscal safety net. She quotes an economist saying “based on Tuesday’s yields, [the Treasury’s] headroom against the current budget rule would fall from £26bn at Rachel Reeves’s spring forecast to £13.8bn before covering any additional spending plans.”

When Badenoch challenged Burnham over tax yesterday, he pointed out that in his first week in office he made two tax-cutting announcements. But he refused to oblige her by ruling out tax rises in the budget.

Today the Resolution Foundation thinktank (whose former chief executive, Torsten Bell, is now a Treasury minister) has published a report saying that, if Burnham wants to raise defence spending, as he proposes, taxes will probably have to rise for ordinary workers. It says:

double quotation markInternational data shows that the rise in employer national insurance contributions (NICs) last year and frozen tax thresholds in the UK have led to the largest annual rise in taxes on average workers across 33 comparable OECD rich countries. Strikingly, however, this was from a very low base – lower than the US, for example. The UK remains in the bottom third of such countries for the level of tax on an average worker, and the effective tax rate on a typical earner is still lower than it was before the financial crisis. Indeed, no country raises more in total tax as a proportion of GDP without also asking more of single average earners. This analysis strongly suggests that any politician promising a bigger state and lower taxes on middle earners is not being realistic. So if we want to increase defence spending, then there is a clear case for paying for this through broad-based tax rises that include typical earners paying more.
With all this on the table, PMQs is likely to be dominated by questions about tax and borrowing.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.15am: Michael Shanks, the energy minister, Ofgem officials and other energy experts give evidence to the Commons energy committee about the electricity market.
9.30am: Stephen Timms, the social security and disability minister, gives evidence to the Commons work and pensions committee.
Morning: Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, holds a press conference in Cardiff ahead of the start of the Senedd year.
Noon: Andy Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.
After 12.30pm: MPs debate the remaining stages of the representation of the people bill.
Afternoon: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, is doing an interview with Chris Mason, the BBC’s political editor, ahead of the party’s conference that starts on Friday.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau referendum approves new constitution that expands president's powers
articles.summary: The sweeping reforms come in the wake of last year's coup and ahead of a proposed return to civilian rule.

blocks.text: Voters in Guinea-Bissau have approved a new constitution that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of general elections later this year.
The referendum was organised by the military government that seized power in the West African nation last November following a disputed election.

Voters have agreed to sweeping reforms allowing the president to appoint and dismiss the ​prime minister and cabinet, create or abolish ministries and dissolve parliament in ⁠the event of a grave political crisis.
The main opposition party boycotted the vote, saying the process lacked adequate political and institutional safeguards and threatened the country's transition back to democracy.
Guinea-Bissau, one of the poorest countries in the world, has experienced at least nine attempted and successful coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974.
The UN has dubbed the country a "narco-state" - its coastline has many uninhabited islands, making it ideal for drug traffickers.

Provisional results announced by the country's electoral commission showed that 70% of voters backed the changes in Sunday's referendum, while 30% voted against them. Turnout was reported at nearly 60%.
The new constitution strengthens the presidency at the expense of the prime minister, altering the balance of power under Guinea-Bissau's semi-presidential system.

Previously, Guinea-Bissau's legislature appointed a prime minister from the parliamentary majority, who then formed a cabinet - an arrangement the ruling military authorities said had contributed to political instability.
The changes now give the president greater authority over the government.
However, the five-year presidential term and two-term limit have been retained.
The military authorities have argued that the changes are necessary to end repeated disputes between presidents and prime ministers.
The new constitution also reduces the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cuts the number of electoral constituencies from 29 to 12.
It introduces new eligibility requirements for presidential candidates, including a provision requiring them to have lived continuously in Guinea-Bissau for the five years before an election.
The changes come ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for December, which the military authorities say are intended to return the country to civilian rule.

But the referendum was strongly opposed by the country's main opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which urged its supporters to boycott the vote.
It warned that the changes risked concentrating too much power in the presidency.
PAIGC leader Domingos Simões Pereira accused those behind the referendum of seeking to undermine democracy and political freedoms.
Some activists told the BBC that the referendum was a mere formality and claimed that 90% of registered voters did not take part.
The referendum follows another turbulent period in Guinea-Bissau's politics.
The military seized power in November 2025 following a disputed presidential election in which then-President Umaro Sissoco Embaló and opposition candidate Fernando Dias both claimed victory.
The junta leaders said they had acted to thwart a plot by unnamed politicians who had "the support of a well-known drug baron" to destabilise the country.
The takeover added Guinea-Bissau to a growing list of western and central African countries that have experienced military coups in recent years.

December's elections will now be an important test of whether the military authorities follow through on their pledge to restore civilian rule and how the expanded powers of the presidency reshape Guinea-Bissau's fragile political system.

articles.title: EU holds talks on response to Leipzig drone attack after Germany formally blames Moscow for incident – Europe live
articles.summary:
Foreign policy chief says drone attack last month ‘had all the hallmarks of state sponsored terrorism’ as she prepares to lead today’s discussions

Britain’s foreign secretary Ed…

blocks.text: Morning opening: EU holds talks on response to Leipzig attack

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia’s attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month “had all the hallmarks of state sponsored terrorism,” as she prepares to lead talks on the bloc’s political reaction.
Kallas will host today’s informal talks between EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, focusing on “what more we can do” after Germany formally blamed Russia for last month’s security incident.

blocks.caption: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas addresses reporters in County Wicklow, Ireland. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: She said the incident should serve as a “wake-up call” for those countries that have been dragging their feet on further sanctions against Russia. “If we want to end this war, we all have to focus our efforts, take it to a new level,” she said.
Separately, the EU and France have summoned top Russian officials to protest against the attack.
Kallas said the discussions will also look at how the EU can further help Ukraine when “Russia is escalating and killing the civilians and causing as much harm as they can.”
Later today, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen will separately meet with Nato’s Mark Rutte, with the Leipzig incident and Ukraine also set to dominate their talks.
I will bring you all the details here.
Elsewhere, Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten will host French president Emmanuel Macron today, who is then expected in Britain for talks with PM Andy Burnham.
It’s Wednesday, 2 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 12m agoRussia's attempts to divide Europe will fail, UK's Miliband says
15m agoRussia 'must live with consequences' of its actions, German minister says
25m agoGermany investigating suspected attempt to disrupt power grid at another substation
26m agoTwo people injured after an explosion near Augsburg train station
26m agoMorning opening: EU holds talks on response to Leipzig attack

blocks.text: Russia's attempts to divide Europe will fail, UK's Miliband says
Britain’s foreign secretary Ed Miliband is also taking part in today’s talks in Ireland.
“We see an attempt by Russia to divide us in Europe and to deter us from our support for Ukraine. And I say very clearly today, on behalf of the United Kingdom, this attempt will fail.”
He says that the UK “will stand shoulder to shoulder with our friends with Ukraine,” as it has since the full-scale invasion in 2022.
He says the UK knows Russia’s tactics “from the past Russian attacks on our soil,” and “these attempts to divide us will not work.”
Russia 'must live with consequences' of its actions, German minister says
Wadephul says he is “impressed by the strong European support” for Berlin’s decision to attribute the Leipzig attack to Russia, with “a great deal of unity” from colleagues.
“It is very important that Russia clearly sees that Europe stands together,” he says.
He says Russia “must understand” that its approach will not work.
He says the German decision to attribute the attack to Russia was “a well-founded opinion and judgment.”
“Russia must now live with the consequences,” he says, pointing to “necessary and appropriate response” proposed yesterday.
Wadephul says that in the coming weeks the EU will be working on expanding its sanctions, which would target “a large number of individuals.”

Let’s go back to Wicklow and listen to German foreign minister Johann Wadephul, who will be briefing his EU counterparts today on the latest in the Leipzig investigation and Berlin’s reasoning for formally naming Russia as responsible for the attempted drone attack.
He’s speaking now.
Germany investigating suspected attempt to disrupt power grid at another substation
Separately, German police are also investigating another attempt to disrupt the country’s energy grid, this time at a electricity substation in Bergheim in the west of the country.
A local police spokesperson said they are “not assuming a technical failure but a deliberate act,” without revealing more details. The region’s power supply was not affected.
Again, like with yesterday’s incident at a substation near a coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg, the issue of attribution here is not straightforward.

AFP notes that German authorities are on high alert for ​attacks on ​vital infrastructure after Berlin blamed ​Russia for an attempted drone attack on a ​Ukrainian cargo ‌plane at ​Leipzig/Halle airport ​last month and ordered a series of measures in response.
But Germany’s electricity grid has been hit by attacks before, including by suspected left-wing militants.
Again, I will keep an eye on updates on this.
Two people injured after an explosion near Augsburg train station
Two people were injured after an unknown object exploded near a train station in the southern German city of Augsburg.
A separate suspicious object was later found nearby, prompting police to temporarily suspend train services and close the station.
But, and that’s an important caveat, local media are reporting that the incident may be linked to organised crime rather than anything else, though authorities are yet to confirm a motive.
I will keep an eye on this for you.

articles.title: Charlie Kirk murder suspect to face potential death penalty
articles.summary: Tyler R., accused of fatally shooting Charlie Kirk, will stand trial on aggravated murder charges after a Utah judge ruled prosecutors had enough evidence to seek the death penalty.

image.caption: Utah prosecutor Ryan McBride presents closing arguments in the preliminary hearing for Tyler R., the man accused of fatally shooting Charlie KirkImage: Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The murder case against Tyler R., the man accused of fatally shooting conservative activist Charlie Kirk last September, is headed to trial, and he could face the death penalty if convicted, under a new ruling.
Utah District Judge Tony Graf ruled late on Tuesday that prosecutors had presented sufficient evidence to proceed, ordering that the defendant be set for trial.
The 23-year-old suspect pleaded not guilty to all seven charges, including aggravated murder, following the ruling. A hearing to schedule the trial date is set for October 23.
What did the prosecutors say?

Prosecutors say Tyler R. fired a single shot from a rooftop more than 400 feet (~122 meters) away, striking 31-year-old Kirk in the neck as he addressed a crowd of more than 3,000 people at Utah Valley University.
A strong supporter of President Donald Trump, Kirk has been credited with motivating young voters to turn out for him in the 2024 US presidential election.

blocks.caption: Charlie Kirk was often referred to as the 'youth whisperer' of Trump's MAGA movementImage: DW

blocks.text: Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court the defendant "lay down in a prone position, and he would have seen this mass of people, of 3,000-plus people there for the event, took aim, put his crosshairs on Charlie Kirk and fired."
McBride argued the shooting "created a great risk of death that anyone would know about."

Prosecutors also pointed to the rifle's additional unfired rounds as evidence that the suspect "came prepared to shoot again," and presented DNA evidence they say ties him to the weapon and to a tool allegedly used to engrave one of the cartridges with the words "Hey Fascist! CATCH!"
What did the defense say?

The defendant's attorneys have argued the case does not meet Utah's legal threshold for aggravated murder, which requires showing that others faced a high probability, not just a possibility, of harm.

Defense attorney Staci Visser told the court, "There is one act. There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim," adding that there was "zero evidence that there was any action taken towards other people."
The defense also challenged the reliability of the prosecution's DNA testing.
Court hears argument for political motive

Prosecutors say the defendant targeted Kirk over his political views, citing a text message in which he allegedly wrote to his roommate, "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out."
A handwritten note he reportedly wrote the roommate, who he was romantically involved with, read: "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it."
However, defense attorney Richard Novak countered that Kirk had spoken "hatefully" about LGBTQ people and that the wording of the message didn't necessarily indicate a political motive.
Charlie Kirk shooting deepens divide in US politics
Kirk family welcomes 'important step' for justice

Kirk's parents and widow, Erika Kirk, who now leads his organization Turning Point USA, attended the hearing. In a statement, the Kirk family said the ruling "marks an important step in our family's pursuit of justice for him."

"Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," read the statement posted by Erika Kirk on social media.

Legal analyst Seth Zuckerman told Reuters he expects the case to go to trial rather than end in a plea deal, saying prosecutors "may not be willing to take the death penalty off the table, and that would probably require a trial."

articles.title: Fake 10 Downing Street listing on Booking.com highlights security failures
articles.summary:
Consumer watchdog Which? set up and accepted payment for fake listing for ‘1 bed apartment in heart of London’

Successive politicians have clawed their way past colleagues over the years to…

blocks.text: Successive politicians have clawed their way past colleagues over the years to call the residence home. Yet in an offer that probably seemed too good to be true, the property site Booking.com has been accused of “systemic security failures” after it was able to set up and accept payment for a fake listing for 10 Downing Street.

A property listed as a “1 bedroom apartment in the heart of London” – with the exact address and a picture of the prime minister’s home – was listed on 18 June by researchers from the consumer watchdog Which?.
The listing, which promised a four-minute walk to the Houses of Parliament, was set up so that users had to request a stay and were unable to reserve and pay automatically.

The booking window opened briefly and closed so that a test could be carried out by a researcher from Which?. The consumer watchdog said a payment for a week-long stay had been processed by the digital travel site that enables users to book hotels and other accommodation as well as flights and car rentals.
The money had still not been refunded more than six weeks after it had been set up, according to Which?, which is associated with the Consumers Association charity.
A fake review was also uploaded to the site, describing the stay as “exceptional” and enjoying the experience of “hanging out with Larry the cat”, in a reference to Downing Street’s resident feline.
Despite Booking.com sending a message saying the review would be checked by a team of moderators, the consumer watchdog said it had been added almost immediately.
The team of researchers were also said to have used Booking.com’s mailing system to send an external URL asking the representative for credit card details to confirm the booking, Which? said.
The watchdog claimed the travel site had told them it had the ability to block URLs being sent through the messaging system if it suspected fraudulent activity, but it had not done so.
The listing was finally removed on 27 August, six weeks after it went live.

Rory Boland, the editor of Which? Travel, said: “If Booking.com’s so-called sophisticated AI systems can’t spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it’s no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily.”
The watchdog said its investigation had “uncovered systemic security failures across the platform” and urged Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, to investigate.
after newsletter promotion

A Booking.com spokesperson said: “This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings on our platform. The property added by Which? was not visible to customers or ‘live’ for the time period referenced.
“We use a range of checks, verification measures and artificial intelligence, which help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours.”
It said that as the property was not open and bookable, some of its automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the fraud listing.

An Ofcom spokesperson said platforms have legal duties obliging them to take down illegal content generated by users once it is known. “Booking.com is not in scope of future rules that will apply to paid-for fraudulent advertising, and any change to that would be a matter for government,” they said.

articles.title: What are Youth Leadership Summits, and why are they in Duterte's trial?
articles.summary: How Army youth summits entered DepEd’s confidential fund paper trail tackled in the impeachment trial.

blocks.text: September 2, 2026 | 3:39pm

MANILA, Philippines — When Vice President Sara Duterte was concurrently education secretary, the department turned to a decades-old Army youth program to account for its P15.54 million in confidential funds.

The money was reported as rewards paid to the Department of Education's supposed informants for the Philippine military's Youth Leadership Summits. The DepEd submitted certifications from Army officers to the Commission on Audit as proof that the information-gathering activities had "succeeded."

During the impeachment trial of Duterte on Tuesday, September 1, Army officers testified that the certifications only established that the summits occurred, but they did not necessarily point to the existence of any informant, reward or confidential-fund expenses for the program.
Col. Manaros Boransing II said Youth Leadership Summits have been conducted since 2002 to discourage students and out-of-school youth from being recruited into insurgent or violent extremist groups.
The programs take on different formats and curricula, but are led by the Philippine Army alongside local government units, schools, local police and other community partners.

Some programs would last three or four days and combined leadership and values formation with team-building and lectures on nation-building, drugs, mental health, teenage pregnancy and insurgent recruitment.

A four-day summit in Borongan City in 2023, for example, listed 67 students and out-of-school youth as beneficiaries of talks on youth delinquency and financial literacy. A three-day program in Galimuyod, Ilocos Sur, meanwhile, covered crime and illegal drugs.
DepEd's role in YLS

Boransing said the Army used its regular civil-military operations budget for personnel and coordination. Local governments generally covered participants’ meals, shirts and activities, while other participating agencies paid their own expenses.

"For Army participants and coordination, it was from the Army, the budget of the Army," he said, describing the setup as "kaniya-kaniyang bayad" or KKB—a cost-sharing arrangement with agencies. LGUs would shoulder costs for youth participants.

For these summits, the DepEd serves as a partner, and not a lead organizer. It fielded subject-matter speakers, secured permission for Army personnel to speak with students and recommended schools as venues.
Boransing said his division received only open-source information from the department, and not confidential or intelligence info.

Col. Magtangol Panopio, also testifying before the Senate court, characterized DepEd's as having a larger info-sharing hand, such as in identifying communities vulnerable to insurgent communism and extremism, drugs and family problems. He could not determine whether such information was transmitted as confidential.

As for the costs, the Army typically spent P30,000 to P60,000 per summit, Boransing said. For eight summits in 2023, the costs would not have exceeded P500,000—nowhere close to the DepEd's supposed confidential spending of P15.54 million.
The Army officer could not attest to the DepEd's supposed spending for informants, saying no funds were transferred to their units to stage any of the activities.
"There was no funding released to the 1st Infantry Division from DepEd, sir, of any source," Boransing said.
The issue of certifications

Rules governing confidential funds, such as COA's Joint Circular No. 2015-01, permit rewards to non-government informants only when supported by evidence that their information resulted in successful information-gathering or surveillance.
DepEd’s April 2024 response to COA said the Army activities were “directly resulting from the information provided by informers.”
For the YLS, however, Boransing said the Army usually relied on its own intelligence units without depending on the DepEd to identify security threats and crucial locations for the summits.

"For the First Infantry Tabak Division? No, sir, they did not provide any confidential or surveillance information," Boransing said, partly in Filipino. "What they give is open-source information about their students."
Yet he issued the certification to the DepEd citing summits successfully staged without knowing it would be used to justify confidential fund spending.

Panopio concurred with Boransing, saying his unit's certification was limited to confirming that the summits occurred: "We did not certify anything about money or funds." — Camille Diola based on reports from Cristina Chi and Ian Laqui
