articles.title: Women's football: Anyomi, London City and the German exodus
articles.summary: Nicole Anyomi has joined Alexia Putellas and other star names in signing for the ambitious English club London City Lionesses. The Germany winger told DW England is a better place to develop her game…

image.caption: Nicole Anyomi has moved clubs and league with the World Cup on the horizonImage: Branislav Racko/IMAGO

blocks.text: The London City Lionesses have existed for less than a decade, have played in England's top flight for just one season and can't play in the Champions League. Yet, having broken the women's transfer record last year, the Lionesses have signed some of the game's biggest stars for the coming season as their ambition becomes ever more apparent.

As well as two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas and her Spanish teammate Mapi Leon, England's Euro 2022 winning goalkeeper Mary Earps and French star Kadidiatou Diani, Germany winger Nicole Anyomi is among the new arrivals.
Anyomi left Eintracht Frankfurt, where she'd scored 50 goals in 101 Bundesliga games over five years, for what she considers a greater challenge in England.
The 'perfect step'
"The next step was to go to the league to compete every single weekend and this is what I see here in this league," she told DW.
"I have some friends who already played in the WSL (Women's Super League) and they told me about the league so I think this will be the perfect step for me."

Anyomi is one of several players to leave Germany's Women's Bundesliga for England this summer. Among them are Anyomi's international teammates Vivien Endemann (Wolfsburg to Liverpool), Selina Cerci (Hoffenheim to Arsenal), Carlotta Wamser (Bayer Leverkusen to Manchester City) and England's Georgia Stanway (Bayern Munich to Arsenal).
Anyomi pointed to the increasing gap in infrastructure, finances and coaching as the primary reasons for the exodus.
"In Germany you have two, three teams who are competing at the top but here in England there are five, six, seven, eight teams.

"Also, the facilities and the staff members. We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."
Germany falling further behind?

With England's national team having won the last two Euros, a competition once dominated by Germany, and no German side having won the Champions League since 2015, there is a concern that Germany rested on its laurels for too long.

In an effort to address this issue, last December, the Frauen-Bundesliga FBL e.V. (Women's Bundesliga Association) was formed. Similar to the DFL, which operates the men's Bundesliga, the FBL is designed to improve the league's marketing and increase revenue. It is to take over operation of the league next July 1.
"They have to bring something, not new, but something different into the league so maybe the players would stay," Anyomi said.

"I think it's an investment thing, but I think now they are building something new, to do different things. I'm going to see this season of course and watch the Bundesliga. I hope they are going to invest more, do more for the league so players also from abroad can come to Germany."

blocks.caption: Bayern Munich have won the last three Bundesliga titles and no side but them or Wolfsburg has won since 2012Image: O. Behrendt/Contrast/IMAGO

blocks.text: Her new club are the foremost example of the changing face of women's football. London City did not exist until 2019 when, effectively, they took over the license of another team, Milwall. Their progress has recently been accelerated by Michelle Kang.

The Korean-American businesswoman is a serial investor in women's football and added London City to an ownership portfolio that includes serial Champions League winners OL Lyonnes and US side Washington Spirit in December 2023. Kang's deep pockets and ambition mean London City are on track to compete at the top end of the WSL within the next few years.
Kang ownership presents possibility and prohibition

But her ownership of OL Lyonnes prohibits London City from playing in the Champions League. UEFA, who organize the tournament, have enshrined laws that mean clubs that are in multi-ownership structures cannot both be in the same competition in the same season. Last season, in the men's game, this led to English side Crystal Palace being demoted from the Europa League to the Europa Conference league.

blocks.caption: Nicole Anyomi believes moving to England was a smart move despite a lack of Champions League football – for nowImage: London City Lionesses

blocks.text: "Why would we want to preserve the sporting integrity of men's football, but not of women's football? It's out of the question," said UEFA's head of women's football and former Germany international, Nadine Kessler earlier this year.
"In any sport you want to preserve sporting integrity, that's the most important thing."
Anyomi, who must recover from a hamstring injury before she can make her debut, said she trusts the club, who have so far "done everything they promised" to find a solution.

But the lack of continental football means fewer chances to make her mark alongside the other new arrivals. Given that the World Cup in Brazil is at the end of the coming season, the move could be seen by some as a risk.

"I did think about that because I know I have to play at the club level, otherwise I won't be selected," she said. "I wanted to go abroad two years ago and I didn't in the end, so I decided to go this summer. I had the feeling this is the right step."
Whether it's to London City, or to the WSL more broadly, she's not the only Bundesliga player to feel that way.
What if men played soccer under women's conditions?

articles.title: Congo’s Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
articles.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures. The…

blocks.text: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it.

“Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance,” DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo.
“Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control,” he added.
Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities.

“This outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it, but it can be stopped,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told journalists last week.
The United Nations has appealed for more funding as humanitarian agencies struggle to keep pace with the increasing number of cases.

“International attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground,” Guterres said, warning that the world “must also overcome another virus — the virus of indifference.”
Vaccination campaign gathers momentum
As researchers continue trials aimed at developing a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain, Congolese authorities have rolled out a vaccination campaign focused on front-line health workers.
The vaccine was originally developed for a different Ebola variant, but officials hope it will provide some protection against the current outbreak.

blocks.caption: Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow

blocks.text: Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses had already arrived in the country.

“We will cover all the provinces that are around Ituri, moving in a ring towards the center of the outbreak, that is to say towards Ituri. But we have enough doses for all healthcare providers,” he said on August 28.
Some health workers remain confident despite uncertainty over how effective the vaccine will be against the Bundibugyo strain.

“It is a vaccine that has already proven itself. We are talking about Ebola Bundibugyo, of Ugandan origin. But the vaccine that they want to administer to us was the vaccine that had succeeded for the Zaire type,” said health worker Arnaud Batumbu.
“Since both cases involve a viral disease, I hope the vaccine will work for us now as well,” he added.
Communities seek protection
Residents in hard-hit areas say they are ready to take the vaccine if it is properly explained to them.
“I will be ready to get vaccinated if only someone explains to me the importance of this vaccination,” Clemency, a student in Tshopo province, told DW.

blocks.caption: Health workers are worried about the spread of the virusImage: Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Others are calling for wider access. “Children need to be vaccinated too. They go back to school; there are many of them in class,” said local resident Carine Lobwadji
Some community members also fear vaccine supplies may not be enough.

“I have learned that this is an insufficient quantity. I ask the authorities to add other doses for Tshopo and that we vaccinate everyone, especially those who will voluntarily agree, since some are afraid,” said Onyeka Treasure, a photographer.
Violence hampers response
The latest outbreak is unfolding against a backdrop of violence and mass displacement in eastern DRC, complicating efforts to stop transmission.
Ebola response teams have reported attacks while carrying out their work, including during operations to safely handle Ebola-related deaths.

“We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives,” Floribert Magene, a member of an Ebola response team, told The Associated Press on Monday after an attack in Ituri province.
Magene said his team was assaulted near Mambasa while responding to a call to secure a body.
Economic toll grows
Beyond the health emergency, the outbreak is worsening economic hardship for many families.
Schools have reopened in towns such as Bukavu and Bunia, but many parents are struggling to afford basic school supplies.
Stationery shop owner Furaha Mpangu Esperance told DW that demand has collapsed as families prioritize food and other essentials.

“In any case, it doesn’t work. The situation is serious because there are no customers. We have even lowered the prices but there is no one to buy. Before, we even sold 10 boxes, 20 boxes a day. Today not even three boxes, not even two! The situation is critical,” he said.
To reduce disruption to education, the government has proposed radio-based learning for children unable to attend school.

“For us, it’s a double objective: to ensure that children continue to go to school, despite the epidemic, and to ensure that distance learning is the device that will help them,” Education Minister Raissa Malu told DW.

blocks.caption: Schools have enforced protective measures, like hand-washingImage: DW

blocks.text: Teachers, however, say many areas lack the infrastructure needed for effective distance learning.

“We, the teachers, are ready, but we don’t have the tools. In sensitive areas, even picking up frequencies is quite a problem,” said Patrick Girinegi, president of the Ituri teachers’ inter-union alliance. “The first-grade children can’t read, nor do the parents. Several schools don’t have printers or computers. How will it go?”
Many students and parents would rather see classrooms remain open with stronger health measures in place.

“It’s easy for me to understand when it’s my teacher himself who explains it to me. Saying that the child stays at home to listen to the radio, I don’t think it’s going to work. We [must] find ways to go to school without contaminating ourselves,” said Viviane Tshipamba, vice-president of the Ituri children’s committee.

Despite the challenges, health authorities point to a positive sign: more than 1,360 people have recovered from Ebola so far. For many Congolese, those recoveries offer hope that with stronger support, increased vaccination rates and improved security, the outbreak can still be brought under control. /dl

articles.title: War and sanctions deepen Iran’s fuel crisis
articles.summary: Only days after Washington announced a new round of economic sanctions on Iran, the country’s gasoline shortage has become increasingly visible on the streets. In cities across Iran, drivers…

blocks.text: Only days after Washington announced a new round of economic sanctions on Iran, the country’s gasoline shortage has become increasingly visible on the streets.

In cities across Iran, drivers are reporting hours-long waits at filling stations. Videos circulating on social media show some people arriving before midnight or sleeping in their cars to secure fuel the following morning. Some stations are closing before serving everyone in line.

The situation is even more difficult for diesel. Truck drivers say lines at filling stations near major cities can stretch for kilometers, forcing them to wait overnight simply to obtain enough fuel to return to work.

Iran already faces a gasoline deficit of roughly 15 million liters (ca. 4 million gallons) a day. War damage, difficulties importing refined products and a tightening US blockade have made an old structural problem much harder to manage.
Hours in line for a few liters
A resident of Karaj, a city west of the capital, Tehran, told DW that some filling stations were limiting individual purchases to around 5 liters (about 1.3 gallons).

“I’m in the gasoline line right now. It took about 45 minutes just to get this far,” he said. “Yesterday I went to several stations. Some were closed, some had no gasoline and others had very long queues.”
He said he returned at 6 a.m. the next morning hoping to avoid the crowds, but again found a long line.
He suspects the shortages are partly being used to prepare public opinion for higher gasoline prices, a claim that could not be independently verified.
For truck drivers, waiting means losing income.

“Our whole life is either spent in the diesel line or on the road,” one driver said. He described sleeping at a station while waiting for a tanker that might arrive around midday and supply only a few dozen trucks.
Another driver said he had been waiting since 8 a.m. after failing to obtain diesel the previous day.
For drivers whose earnings depend directly on keeping their vehicles moving, every lost day adds to rising insurance, tire, oil, repair and maintenance costs.
Is Iran adulteratingits gasoline?
The shortage has coincided with the use of methanol in domestically produced gasoline.
Vahid Ghaneifard, chief executive of Persian Gulf Star Oil Company, recently confirmed that the refinery had begun testing methanol as an oxygenate in its gasoline.
The company says methanol makes up around 0.5% of the mixture. Iran’s refining authorities say the national fuel standard permits methanol concentrations of up to 3%.
Officials insist the trial complies with technical requirements. But the timing has fueled public suspicion.
Videos shared online show motorists holding bottles of unusually clear fuel and claiming that gasoline quality has deteriorated.
Some have alleged that water or excessive alcohol is being mixed into supplies. The allegations have not been independently corroborated.

There has, however, been at least one confirmed incident involving water contamination. In the city of Rafsanjan, local authorities acknowledged that water had been mixed with gasoline at a filling station after videos showed cars and motorcycles experiencing problems.
Officials said the incident resulted from a technical fault and was being investigated.
Distrust over fuel quality grows
For motorists already facing shortages, isolated incidents can reinforce wider fears.

A Tehran resident told DW he had spent about 1 billion tomans — roughly $5,250 (€4,529) at current exchange rates — repairing his car after its crankshaft failed. He believed poor-quality gasoline had caused the damage, though such a connection has not been independently established.
He said he was reluctant to publicly protest.
Another resident in Rey, south of Tehran, told DW that motorists had gathered outside a filling station after several cars were allegedly damaged following refueling.
The concern is not simply technical, as it reflects a deeper collapse of trust between consumers and authorities at a time when the government is also discussing higher gasoline and diesel prices.
Tehran has argued that the current subsidy system encourages excessive consumption and smuggling and imposes an unsustainable burden on state finances.
But consumers point to other issues such as inefficient cars, inadequate public transport and incomes that have failed to keep pace with inflation.
Is a price increase in the works?
Economist Hassan Mansour believes the government is preparing the political ground for higher energy prices.

Officials have repeatedly argued that Iranian gasoline prices are artificially low, that large volumes are smuggled abroad and that the economy consumes far more energy per unit of output than comparable countries.
The proposed solution is to bring domestic fuel prices closer to international levels.
“Once again, the government finds itself preparing the ground for raising the price of energy carriers,” Mansour told DW.
But the problem runs deeper than subsidized gasoline.

Mansour pointed to the financial condition of Iran’s oil industry. Budget documents indicate that the National Iranian Oil Company has tens of billions of euros in debt to the central bank and commercial banks, while the company also owes substantial sums to the National Development Fund and faces major tax liabilities.
When these debts cannot realistically be repaid, Mansour argued, they weaken state finances and contribute indirectly to currency instability and inflation.
Raising gasoline prices could, therefore, serve both as a demand management measure and a source of additional revenue.
A politically dangerous choice
The government has few easy options.
While imports are harder to finance and transport, domestic production is struggling to keep pace with consumption.
Increasing output quickly requires investment and technology, while reducing consumption means either rationing fuel more aggressively or raising prices. Yet both carry political risks.
Iranian authorities remember what happened in November 2019, when a sudden gasoline price increase triggered nationwide protests followed by a deadly crackdown and an internet shutdown.
Today, the economic environment is considerably more fragile.
The war has damaged infrastructure, international sanctions are tightening and household purchasing power has fallen sharply. Long fuel lines are just another source of frustration.
For Tehran, raising prices might help reduce the gasoline deficit.
But doing so while people are already waiting overnight for fuel could turn an energy shortage into another crisis of public anger, which is something far more difficult to control. /dl

articles.title: Prosecutors weigh skipping bribery article to shorten Duterte trial
articles.summary: House may trim presentation of Sara Dutere's case to avoid trial stretching into 2027.

blocks.text: September 2, 2026 | 2:58pm

Members of the prosecution panel Rep. Jinky Luistro (L), Rep. Joel Chua (C) and private counsel Lorna Kapunan confer during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutors are considering skipping one of the four articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte for the Senate trial and moving from the current confidential-funds charge directly to the unexplained wealth article.

Saying the panel is aiming to finish presenting their case by October, Rep. Joel Chua admitted the bribery charge may take a back seat for the body to proceed instead to the larger allegations on Duterte's supposed wealth.
"Well, that is possible," Chua said in a TV5 interview on Wednesday, September 2.
Chua pointed to the previous grave threats and the ongoing confidential fund debates as already substantial.

"We are looking at the strong arguments on our two articles. So, we would just add another article that we think we really can't skip—that is, the unexplained wealth, which everyone is looking forward to," Chua said in Filipino.
Where the trial is at now
The prosecution first presented Article IV, involving Duterte's alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.

It is now presenting Article I, which accuses Duterte of misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of P612.5 million in confidential funds released to the Office of the Vice President and Department of Education, when Duterte was secretary.
Former DepEd undersecretary, chief of staff and spokesperson Michael Wesley Poa is currently on the witness stand as prosecutors examine the department's use and liquidation of confidential funds.

If prosecutors finish Article I and move directly to Article II on unexplained wealth, Article III, which accuses Duterte of bribery and graft involving alleged cash payments to DepEd officials, could be left out of the prosecution's presentation.

The unexplained wealth article accuses Duterte of amassing assets disproportionate to her and hur husband's lawful income, failing to fully disclose assets and financial interests in her statements of assets, liabilities and net worth, and continuing business interests while serving as vice president.
Avoiding a prolonged trial
Chua said prosecutors expect to finish presenting evidence on the confidential-funds article in the next few trial days before moving on to another charge.
"We expect that by next week, we're done," he said in the same interview.
The prosecution does not want proceedings to stretch into 2027, he said, particularly because Duterte's defense team will still have to present its own evidence after the House rests its case.
"We also don't want a protracted hearing. We don't want that stretch this out to next year," Chua said.
He floated a timeline under which the prosecution could finish by October and the defense by November, noting that the two sides may call some of the same witnesses.

"So, we hope by December, we already have a decision from the impeachment court," Chua said, referring to the body of senator-judges. The panel needs 16 votes to oust Duterte from office and ban her from future public posts she might pursue.

The four articles approved by the House accuse Duterte of offenses involving confidential funds, unexplained wealth, alleged bribery of DepEd officials and alleged threats against Marcos and others. — with reports from Cristina Chi

articles.summary: Coast guard vessels and a helicopter are searching for 10 missing crew members off the coast of Istanbul. Authorities say they lost contact after the bulk carrier crashed into a chemical tanker off…

image.caption: The 90-meter (295-foot) cargo ship Tugberk Imamoglu was traveling from Turkey’s Iskenderun to Eregli in the Black SeaImage: DHA

blocks.text: Turkish authorities are searching for 10 people aboard a cargo ship that sank after a collision with another vessel in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul early Wednesday.

"Due to the Tugberk Imamoglu vessel failing to respond to any calls and the crew members' mobile phones not being answered ... it is believed the Tugberk Imamoglu dry cargo vessel has sunk," the Transport Ministry's maritime directorate said on X.
The bulk carrier collided with the Alsu, a chemical tanker, at around 3 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) off Istanbul's western Silivri district, the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement.
What else do we know about the missing ship?
The 90-meter (295-foot) Turkish-flagged bulk carrier was en route to the Black Sea ​port ‌of Karadenizeregli from Iskenderun when the collision happened, the Istanbul governor's office said.
According to the maritime directorate, it was carrying 4,199 tons of coiled steel.

The 91-meter (298-foot) Turkish-flagged Alsu, was sailing from Kocaeli, east of Istanbul, to Aliaga on the Aegean coast. It did not appear to have suffered any damage in the collision, the governor's office said.
Coast guard vessels and a helicopter are scouring the area for the missing ship.

articles.title: Will Bangladesh join the Mecca defense alliance?
articles.summary: There has been widespread speculation about Bangladesh becoming part of a mutual defense deal struck last month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. But the South Asian country says it has yet to…

blocks.text: There has been widespread speculation about Bangladesh becoming part of a mutual defense deal struck last month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. But the South Asian country says it has yet to receive an invitation.

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, ​signed into force in early August, ​is intended to strengthen collective ​deterrence against any act of aggression. It stipulates that an ​armed attack against any of the three countries would be regarded ​as an attack on all.
Some analysts believe the pact has already changed the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East and South Asia.

“Although it is a collective defense understanding, from a strategic perspective it is primarily an initiative to maintain the regional balance of power and advance the respective interests of the participating states,” ​Navine Murshid, a political science and sociology professor at North South University in Dhaka, told DW.
Bangladesh govt. in favor of Mecca pact
Any move by Bangladesh to join, however, could complicate its foreign relations, particularly with neighboring India.
The two countries share a 4,096-kilometer (2,545-mile) land border, and have strong cultural and economic ties.
India, a fierce rival of Pakistan, sheltered many Bangladeshi refugees and provided military support to Bangladesh during its independence war against Islamabad in 1971.

However, ties between New Delhi and Dhaka have become increasingly contentious since a deadly student-led uprising in 2024 toppled then Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was considered a close ally of the Indian government.
Now living in exile in India, Hasina has since been convicted in absentia for crimes against humanity during the uprising. She has denied the charges.

blocks.caption: Will Bangladesh join the Mecca defense alliance?

blocks.text: Bangladesh’s current government, headed by the center-right Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), is in favor of the Mecca agreement.
“We view this pact positively,” Bangladeshi Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman said in response to a question in parliament last week.
But he insisted that the question of Bangladesh joining the pact, or even considering membership, had not yet arisen, as that would depend on the intentions of its current members.
“If they express an intention to include Bangladesh in the pact, we will certainly consider it positively,” he said.
When asked about the remarks made by Bangladeshi officials, India said the pact had implications for its national security and that it was closely monitoring the situation.

“We continue to follow all developments that have a bearing on India’s security and take all necessary steps to safeguard it,” Randhir Jaiswal, a spokesperson for India’s Ministry of External Affairs, told reporters in New Delhi last week.
Competing geopolitical interests
Analysts said Dhaka needs to consider its interests carefully before making any move to join the joint defense pact.

“The scope for direct conventional interstate war or military conflict in South Asia is limited. Therefore, the primary role of such an agreement is not confined to conducting border wars,” said Murshid.
“In international relations, its significance lies mainly in strengthening bargaining power and maintaining one’s position against the influence of other regional countries.”
Murshid added that Pakistan’s interest in bringing Bangladesh closer through this agreement “is driven by geographical and political considerations.”

“For India, the security of the Siliguri Corridor and its eastern frontier are important considerations,” she said, referring to India’s narrow land link to its northeastern states, which wraps around Bangladesh to the north. “If Pakistan’s defense-related influence in Bangladesh were to increase, New Delhi could view this as a development capable of affecting the regional balance of relationships.”
In such circumstances, Bangladesh would have to clearly define what it would and would not do by joining this alliance, she explained.

“In particular, a clear position would be necessary regarding Bangladesh’s role if a military conflict were to arise between India and Pakistan. Taking Pakistan’s side during such a conflict could create political and diplomatic pressures for Dhaka that may exceed Bangladesh’s capacity to manage,” she stressed.

Dhaka-based former diplomat M Humayun Kabir sees no reason for Bangladesh to join the pact. “Bangladesh has not joined any military alliance over the past 50 to 55 years. As far as I am concerned, I believe that position remains unchanged to this day,” he told DW.

“They are talking about a regional security arrangement, but the region in question concerns Pakistan and the Middle East. We are not part of that region or geographical area. Bangladesh is located in the eastern part of South Asia. Therefore, there is no direct geographical rationale for Bangladesh to participate in such a military alliance,” he added.
Would Bangladesh benefit from joining the pact?
Murshid stressed that Bangladesh needed to develop its own defense infrastructure and security systems sustainably.
She believes that becoming part of an international security agreement could help modernize Dhaka’s defense capabilities and facilitate access to military technology.

“The text of the agreement does not directly mention trade, labor markets or economic relations. However, it is natural for economic elements to become linked with a security framework, a phenomenon known in international relations as issue linkage,” she said.

However, Kabir fears joining the pact could limit Bangladesh’s geopolitical options and recommended a balanced approach. “We contribute to peacekeeping missions around the world under the auspices of the United Nations, and that is important to us. Our economy is interconnected with many different countries in various ways, which is also important. Our workforce is present in countries across the world, and that, too, is an important consideration,” he said.
“Therefore, before making any decision on this issue, we must take into account the many different dimensions and forms of our national interests.” /dl

articles.title: Germany news: Police probe suspected power station attacks
articles.summary: Police are investigating after homemade projectiles were used to damage power lines in eastern Germany. This comes amid suspicion of sabotage at another power station in the west of the country. DW…

image.caption: Police combed the a substation in Bergheim, North Rhine-Westphalia on WednesdayImage: Thilo Schmuelgen/REUTERS

blocks.text: September 2, 2026
Sabotage probe opened in second power station attack near Cologne

North Rhine-Westphalia’s Interior Minister Herbert Reul on Wednesday said an incident at a power station in Bergheim near Cologne is preliminarily being investigated as an act of "anti-constitutional sabotage," using a German legal term applied for criminal acts aimed against the order of the state.

On Tuesday night, police were called to the Amprion substation in Bergheim after bright flashes of light were reportedly visible. A short circuit affected several power lines, but officials said power supply to citizens was not affected.

It was the second incident involving attempts at damaging electricity infrastructure in 24 hours. On Tuesday morning, power lines at a substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg hundreds of kilometers away were damaged by a projectile.
Officials have yet to identify potential suspects involved in either incident.

blocks.caption: Police search for clues on Wednesday after a second power station incident Image: Thilo Schmuelgen/REUTERS

blocks.text: Based on the investigation so far, Reul said the investigation is looking at whether the sabotage attackoriginated from abroad or had a far-left extremist motive.

Last year in Berlin, a far-left extremist network known as the "Vulkangruppe" carried out multiple sabotage attacks on power grids and energy infrastructure in and around Berlin, leaving thousands without power for nearly a week in the middle of winter.
"Now we need to investigate," Reul said. "This was intentional; it was a crime," Ruel said.
"More sabotage, more hybrid attacks ... interference like this is not happening far away, it's happening right on our doorstep," Reul told a press conference.
"And anyone who acts this way is not just trying to hit cables; they're trying to hit our country," he added.

articles.title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
articles.summary:
Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every…

blocks.text: Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.

blocks.caption: Young farm workers harvesting cotton in a field near Boromo in Burkina Faso. Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.

Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”

The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
after newsletter promotion

Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”

Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.

Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.

Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.

Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

articles.title: UK must end all trade with Israel, says co-founder of BDS movement
articles.summary:
Exclusive: sanctions against ministers and settler groups are ‘smoke and mirrors cop-out’ says Omar Barghouti

Britain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to…

blocks.text: Britain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to take bigger steps than halting trade with illegal Israeli settlements or imposing further sanctions, Omar Barghouti, the co-founder of the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement has said.

He described sanctions against individual settler groups or extremist ministers as a “smoke and mirrors cop-out and distraction” from the UK’s legal obligation under international law to end all support for Israel, including arms exports, trade deals and academic relations that “may directly or indirectly enable Israel’s illegal occupation” of Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem.
The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised on Tuesday to introduce a “comprehensive reset” of the UK’s policy on Israel in the coming weeks.

It has been reported that the UK is preparing to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Miliband told the Commons the government was looking at how to stop British companies “financing, constructing or advertising new settlements”.

Miliband has called plans for the E1 settlement, which would involve the construction of 3,400 houses through the heart of the West Bank, unacceptable and destructive, adding that, by cutting across the territory, critics say it will render a two-state solution impossible.
Tenders for the settlements are due to be handed out, potentially irreversibly, days before the Israeli elections on 27 October.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council have warned Miliband that a UK ban on trade with settlements may fuel antisemitism in the UK.
A third group of British Jews, Yachad, also met Miliband to highlight “the growing concerns of many British Jews about the entrenchment of occupation and effective annexation of the West Bank”.
Barghouti, an influential advocate for Palestinian rights for more than 20 years, said the litmus test for human rights law and the west still lay in Palestine.

He said: “In July 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Israel’s entire occupation of Gaza, and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is illegal and amounts to a violation of the racial segregation and apartheid prohibitions under international law.
“Dozens of UN human rights experts have said to fulfil those obligations a set of minimal steps are required: a full military embargo, export import, dual-use transfer and transit.
“They also said you have to end all trade, diplomatic and economic relations and academic relations that enable Israel’s illegal occupation.”
Barghouti added: “Further in January 2024, the ICJ said there is a plausible case of the violation of Palestinian rights under the Genocide Convention.

“The ICJ decided there is a plausible risk of genocide that is sufficient to trigger third state responsibilities. But UK government lawyers seem to ignore that part of the ruling and say the court has not ruled on genocide.
“But the genocide convention is very clear – where there is a risk, the obligation to prevent is triggered, and how do you prevent a genocide? You stop enabling it. You end all forms of complicity.”

The Israeli embassy referred to the warning by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools.” He added: “The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”
after newsletter promotion
Explaining why he regards UK sanctions as “totally performative”, Barghouti said: “They have no concrete effect in holding Israel to account or pressuring it to comply with international law.”
He added: “Israel has de facto annexed the occupied Palestinian territory, making it near impossible [to] differentiate so-called settlement goods and services.”
Pressed whether the BDS movement is trying to change the minds of Israelis through economic force, Barghouti insisted sanctions have to be legal and ethical.

“They have to target the perpetrators, whether entities or individuals that are involved in crimes, especially international crimes. They are actually measures of accountability, not sanctions that simply say settlers shall not have vacations in London.”

Despite South Africa feeling forced to return to the ICJ to point out Israel is not complying with court orders, he said he retained his faith in international law – for all its colonial origins – arguing it was not something engraved in stone, but dynamic.
“Humanity has agency to evolve and expand international law. We in the BDS movement have been pushing the envelope of its interpretation.”

Barghouti added: “So, in the BDS movement, we try to hold states, corporations and institutions accountable to end their own complicity in genocide rather than just wait for the messiah of international law to come and save us.
“We definitely need international law, just as we need to maintain the ethical high ground. Both are necessary, but not sufficient. We need people power to achieve liberation. There is no other way.”

articles.title: South Korea jails disabled care home head for sexually assaulting residents
articles.summary: The man, surnamed Kim, was handed a 15-year prison term for abusing three residents at the facility near Seoul.

blocks.text: A South Korean court has jailed the former head of a disabled care home for sexually assaulting multiple residents, in a case that shocked the nation.
The man, surnamed Kim, was handed a 15-year prison term for abusing three residents at the Saekdongwon facility in Incheon City, west of Seoul.
Police started investigating Kim after one of his victims, a woman with a severe intellectual disability, came forward in February last year.
The case has prompted the government to inspect 1,507 care facilities for disabled people across the country, where 33 cases of suspected abuse were found.
South Korean Prime Minister Kim Min-seok had described the abuse at Saekdongwon as "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".
An in-depth assessment of residents commissioned by Ganghwa County found that 20 current and former female residents may have experienced sexual abuse.
Many in South Korea have asked how such a case could still occur, especially after laws were strengthened in 2011 to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.
Some have also raised questions on how the director's actions could have gone undetected for so long.
Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close, while Incheon City officials revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.
However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.
The foundation has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence.

articles.title: Queensland police investigate after 5,500 sheep worth $1.7m stolen from farm
articles.summary:
Police say the sheep were stolen from a property 830km west of Brisbane between February and May

  • Get our breaking…

blocks.text: Queensland police are investigating after about 5,500 Dorper sheep worth more than $1.7m were allegedly stolen from a western Queensland farm.
Police said the sheep were stolen from a property outside Blackall, about 830km west of Brisbane, between February and May this year.
Detective Sen Sgt Paul Elliot, from the rural and stock crime squad, said the sheep had an estimated value of about $1.7m (£899,000).
They are fitted with white National Livestock Identification System tags and are Dorper sheep, a breed with white wool but a black face. Both ewes and rams were taken.
Elliot urged anyone with information about the theft or who had seen Dorper sheep matching the description in the area to come forward.

“Livestock theft investigations can be complex, often spanning large geographical areas, which is why we work closely with producers, saleyards, transport operators and industry stakeholders to identify offenders and disrupt criminal activity,” he said.
The AgForce general president, Shane McCarthy, said it was a “a concerning amount of sheep that have been stolen” and would have a significant effect on the farm’s bottom line.
“We’re seeing a concerning rise in the number of incidents like this happening across the state,” he said. “We would trust that the police are taking these matters very, very seriously.”

He said a sheep theft of that scale would require a plan, time and more than one person. Sheep rustlers will sometimes take a group into a property where they can be bred to gain the value of their progeny and then slowly sold to abattoirs over time.
Thefts are often discovered at the abattoir, he said.

“I would say that it’s been thought out for a while,” he said. “I would suggest that one or two sheep here and there, even up to you know 10 or so sheep, is opportunistic. When we’re talking these numbers, they’re organised.”
It is not yet clear how the sheep were stolen, such as being loaded on to several trucks or mustered.
after newsletter promotion
Dorpers are bred to be eaten, not for wool.
The Blackall-Tambo mayor, Andrew Martin, said the herd was probably not all taken in one night.
“I’m suspecting a number of smaller hits and sneaking them off to the abattoir or whatever it is they’re doing with them,” he said.
Farms in some parts of Queensland can rival the size of some countries. Stock theft is typically discovered during a muster.

Martin, who has farmed Dorper sheep, said some properties have as many as 25,000 sheep. It is possible to lose thousands by them escaping, from an animal attack or just miscounting them, without noticing for a long period of time, he said.
“This is an age-old problem. Potty dodging is a bit of an art, and it’s been going on ever since potties were there to be dodged,” he said, using Australian slang for stock theft.

articles.title: ‘We have had enough’: thousands of University of Sydney staff walk off the job over AI and job security
articles.summary: Hundreds of university staff were stationed at picket lines, calling for stronger protections around the use of AI

blocks.text: The same week union members at the University of Sydney agreed to a 24-hour strike, staff received the results of an internal survey.
In the faculty of arts and social sciences, 0% agreed with the statement: “I trust the University of Sydney to act in the best interests of staff, students and the broader community.”

It was the issue of trust, alongside longstanding concerns over staff protections from artificial intelligence, workload fairness and job security, that saw about 2,000 members to walk off the job on Wednesday.
From 7am, about 500 people were stationed at picket lines at each of the inner Sydney campus’s entrances, armed with flags, banners and megaphones.
The University of Sydney advised students “almost all” scheduled classes would move online as a result of the strike, while others were rescheduled or cancelled.

Peter Chen, the branch president of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) at the University of Sydney, said management had rebuffed the union “at every opportunity” to enforce appropriate protections around the use of AI.
“Higher education is the canary in the coalmine,” he said. “Where we go on AI … will travel through the rest of the economy.”

The New South Wales division secretary of the NTEU, Vince Caughley, said the University of Sydney’s own green paper advised AI was the most “fundamental transformation” education had seen, pointing to AI chatbots that were already being used to help teach online-only classes at other universities.
“We are asking for best practice, we are asking for due diligence,” he said. “Not their own commercialisation aims and certainly not the interest of venture capital.”

The union was confident it would reach an agreement with management within the year but had concerns over the lack of senior leadership at the table, including the provost, Prof Annamarie Jagose. The last bargaining process represented the longest running industrial action at an Australian university, and the prospect of future strikes remained active.
A spokesperson for the University of Sydney said it was “continuing to engage” with the union and maintained industrial action was “premature”.
“We agree using AI ethically requires a human-centred approach, and our … principles and guardrails that govern use have been developed in consultation with our community,” they said.
“We support many of the objectives of the unions’ claims, but believe it’s more appropriate to implement many of these through relevant policies, instead of in the Enterprise Agreement.”

There are broader concerns, some interlinked and widespread in the sector. Growing class sizes and reduced student satisfaction. A new proposal for teaching-only roles with no research component or scope for future growth.

Prof Laura Shepherd in the school of social and political sciences is part of the bargaining team and said students often sacrificed a “huge amount” to come to the university, including spending $50,000 on degrees.
after newsletter promotion
“They come here … for quality and access to research leaders,” she said. “I think we should be very ashamed if we allow anything in the enterprise agreement that threatens that.”

The University of Sydney’s NTEU branch is the largest in Australia, and the university has long been a hotbed for activism. As management approaches its fifth month of bargaining, it is also grappling with continued opposition to its response to Gaza and restrictions on protest.

New restrictions were brought in as a result of the university’s pro-Palestine encampment in 2024, which received intense scrutiny during this year’s royal commission. On Wednesday, keffiyehs and pro-Palestine banners stood out among purple NTEU flags and signage.

The Student Representative Council was also striking in solidarity with staff and picketing online classes. Its education officer, Dana Kafina, said the university’s “draconian” protest restrictions were a motivation.
“In the wake of … suppressions of free speech and activism, and some of the lowest rates of student and graduate satisfaction in the country, we have had enough,” she said.
Despite the presence of campus security and police, the picket lines had a jovial atmosphere. Some blasted music on speakers, others banged drums and chanted with abandon.
Kurt Iveson, a professor of geography, was among them, running a quiz on his megaphone as, behind him, students sold baked goods to raise funds for lost income of strikers.
Iveson has been with the university for 20 years, and wants “meaningful protections” that do not outlaw AI but ensure “the tech is serving our purpose, rather than us serving the tech”.
“All of us on the picket line today are here because we care so much about the education and research we do,” he said.

articles.title: After flood-control freeze, Senate panel eyes funds to finish abandoned works
articles.summary: Senate finance panel eyes completing unfinished projects after this year's funding freeze.

blocks.text: September 2, 2026 | 1:29pm
People stand along a flooded street due to the rains brought by the southwest monsoon in Manila on August 17, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — A year after flood-control spending was frozen in response to a massive corruption scandal, the powerful Senate finance committee is backing its return in the 2027 budget, but only to finish projects already underway.

The approach would keep the door shut on new flood-control projects while restoring money for unfinished works. Committee chair JV Ejercito said the blanket freeze left gaps exposed by the recent widespread flooding in Central Luzon and Metro Manila.

Speaking at a Senate briefing Tuesday, September 1, Ejercito said his committee would maintain its position against funding new flood-control projects under the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget.

"I think we have to resume, but only the uncompleted projects. We should finish the flood-control projects that were not completed... There will be no new flood-control projects," Ejercito said in Filipino.

Funding for new locally funded flood-control projects was withheld from the 2026 budget after investigations into alleged ghost, substandard and anomalous projects involving public officials and private contractors.
Ejercito said the consequences of leaving flood-control projects unfinished could be seen in the recent habagat flooding that submerged parts of Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan and Metro Manila.

For 2027, the Department of Public Works and Highways proposed around P107.4 billion for flood-control projects. The National Expenditure Program, meanwhile, provides P103.45 billion for the agency's Flood Management Program.
Infrastructure master plan
Ejercito also renewed his push for the Masterplan for Infrastructure and National Development (MIND) Act, which seeks to institutionalize a long-term national blueprint for infrastructure projects.

"This will serve as the blueprint or direction for all our infrastructure programs in the future and would transcend several presidencies. Hopefully, even if this has not yet been passed, the budget hearings can already move toward that kind of long-term planning," Ejercito said.

Ejercito said a national infrastructure master plan could help the Philippines catch up with its Southeast Asian neighbors while reducing opportunities for another corruption scandal involving public works.

"So, we hit two birds with one stone. Hopefully, with the MIND bill, we will be able to catch up with our ASEAN neighbors in infrastructure while also preventing corruption scandals as large as the flood-control scam," he said.

articles.title: Japan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streets
articles.summary:
Speed limit dropped from 60km/h for around 70% of general roads in the hope of making narrow streets of crowded cities safer

Drivers on residential roads in

blocks.text: Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.
The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.

Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.

The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.
Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.

While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.
The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.

Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.

“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

articles.title: Israel expanding presence in Lebanon, officials say, as BBC visits occupied areas
articles.summary: A BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force, which says Israeli troops are fortifying positions and continuing demolitions.

blocks.text: Israel expanding presence in Lebanon, officials say, as BBC visits occupied areas
Watch: BBC sees Israeli military presence in southern Lebanon
By
Middle East correspondentReporting fromsouthern Lebanon

The drive on the highway by the Mediterranean in southern Lebanon, near the border with Israel, is scenic and, these days, desolate. Crops lie abandoned and buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes, too many to count, are in ruins.

Near the town of Naqoura, a Lebanese military checkpoint, painted in the white-and-red colours of the national flag, is the last visible sign of the state's presence. Soldiers are positioned behind concrete walls, but the road is empty. A few minutes further south, around a dozen Israeli flags indicate the start of occupied territory. Unless authorised by Israel, no-one can enter.

This part of the country is the heartland of Lebanon's Shia Muslim community, from which Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed militia and political party, gets most of its support. It has seen three invasions by the Israeli military in wars against the group in the last two decades alone. The most recent started in March, after Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel following the killing of the Iranian supreme leader, at the start of the US and Israel's war against Iran.

Last month, a BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, known as Unifil, which is one of the only ways to visit the area under Israeli control. There, as it did in Gaza, Israel has flattened entire villages, and air strikes and demolitions have continued even after a ceasefire was announced in June.

blocks.caption: Image caption, An Israeli soldier at a checkpoint established in a residential building near the Unifil headquarters in Naqoura

blocks.text: Image source, Neha Sharma/BBC
An Israeli soldier at a checkpoint established in a residential building near the Unifil headquarters in Naqoura

Led by Finnish troops who are part of Unifil, the convoy was escorting civilians to and from Christian villages near the border. Those communities were spared from Israel's attacks and invasion during the war and, with the surrounding areas now under occupation, are now cut off from the rest of the country. Our presence was allowed by the Israeli military through a deconfliction mechanism with the UN.

The strip of land currently controlled by Israel constitutes around 5% of Lebanese territory and, in some places, extends 10km (six miles) from the border. Driving along the wall that separates the two countries, we saw service roads built by Israel after the invasion, intense movement of Israeli soldiers and residential buildings that were being used by them. Some were covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones.
We also heard Israeli surveillance drones in the sky and explosions in the distance, possibly from demolitions being carried out by Israel in villages that are under occupation.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israeli soldiers drive on a road along the wall separating Lebanon and Israel

blocks.text: Israeli soldiers drive on a road along the wall separating Lebanon and Israel

In a visit to occupied southern Lebanon last month, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said he had instructed the military to "take all necessary steps to prepare for a long-term presence in the area". Israeli officials say their goal is to establish what they call a "security zone" to protect communities in northern Israel from rockets and drones that have been fired by Hezbollah from southern Lebanon, as well as a possible ground invasion.

According to Unifil, the Israeli military has established four new bases in the invaded areas, bringing the number of such positions to nine. Israeli forces had remained in five points after invading southern Lebanon during the previous war against Hezbollah in 2024, in violation of the deal that ended that conflict.

"In the past months, we've seen the consolidation and fortification of Israeli positions, construction of protective infrastructure, and other engineering works," Kandice Ardiel, a Unifil spokeswoman, said. "We have [also] observed what appear to be Israeli civilian personnel carrying out demolition and engineering activities in support of military activities in south Lebanon."

Human rights groups say some of Israel's actions in southern Lebanon amount to the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure, a possible war crime. Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese remain displaced, without knowing when, or if, they will be able to return.

In response to our questions, the Israeli military said the buildings that had been destroyed were used by Hezbollah for military purposes, and that it operated in accordance with international law. It did not respond to other specific questions about its actions in the occupied areas.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some of the houses used by the Israeli military are covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones

blocks.text: Some of the houses used by the Israeli military are covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones

In June, the US and Iran announced a preliminary deal aimed at ending their conflict, which included a cessation of the violence in Lebanon. Since then, a Lebanese intelligence official told me, Lebanon's military has recorded more than 5,000 violations of the deal by Israel, including air strikes, drone attacks, shelling and near-daily incursions of Israeli soldiers into Lebanese territory beyond the area under occupation, the so-called Yellow Line.

As it does in Gaza, the Israeli military justifies some of its attacks in Lebanon as operations against what it describes as immediate threats. In many cases, however, it is not clear how immediate these alleged threats are or if there is any threat at all. Hezbollah, which is considered a terrorist organisation by countries including the UK and the US, has not carried out attacks against Israel since the ceasefire came into force, but has targeted Israeli troops operating inside Lebanese territory.

"[The Israelis] are expanding their presence [in Lebanon]. They've [also] been setting areas ablaze, demolishing houses while the bombing continues, despite the ceasefire," the Lebanese intelligence official said. "It's clear that they don't want anyone to go back [to those villages] in the coming year, or even years. This isn't only about Hezbollah. This is about preventing people from returning."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Entire villages along the border have been destroyed by Israel

blocks.text: Entire villages along the border have been destroyed by Israel

Israeli officials have conditioned a withdrawal from Lebanon on Hezbollah's disarmament, something the Lebanese government cannot deliver without the group's consent. Hezbollah, observers say, is still a significant military force despite the setbacks in the recent wars. Both countries have held direct talks that resulted in a framework agreement brokered by the US: Israel would pull out of certain areas, called "pilot zones", where Lebanese army soldiers would be deployed and Hezbollah's disarmament would be verified.

Hezbollah opposes the efforts – the group's leader, Naim Qassem, called them "surrender with humiliation" last week – and says any discussion about its weapons should only happen after a full Israeli withdrawal. Israel, for its part, has claimed that the Lebanese national military, which rejects the use of force against the group saying this could pit Lebanese against Lebanese, has not done enough.
The plan has seen no progress, and there is no expectation of any significant change before the Israeli election at the end of October.

"The idea of the 'pilot zones' seems to be dead until the context changes," a European diplomat familiar with the situation told me. "It seems we're heading to a Gaza-like situation. The Israelis are entrenching themselves... and are here to stay, for now."

articles.title: Ray Hadley used homophobic slur against Alan Jones after 2GB withdrew offer of $4m breakfast radio gig, court hears
articles.summary:
Hadley is giving evidence in trial of former 2GB rival Jones, 85, who has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges

  • Get our

blocks.text: Broadcaster Ray Hadley has told a Sydney court he used a homophobic slur and derogatory names when talking about his colleague Alan Jones, after 2GB withdrew a secret offer of a $4m contract to take over Jones’s coveted breakfast slot.
Hadley agreed under cross-examination by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC that he told police in 2019 that Jones had recruited colleagues at 2GB to “dig up some dirt” on him.
Jones is on trial over 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching involving six men. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty.
On his second day giving evidence at Downing Centre local court, Hadley testified that a colleague had told him Jones had “marshalled the troops and said ‘Dig up some dirt on Hadley’”.

Hadley in 2019 had walked into Jones’s office after being accused of an unrelated assault against a colleague, and called the breakfast host “a cunt and a dog”, according to a police statement from the time that was raised in court .
The assault allegation against Hadley was dropped when 2GB CCTV showed nothing had happened, Hadley told Jones’s trial.
Hadley agreed that he had “an animosity towards [Jones] at that time”. He said he often called him a “grub”, and that in a text exchange shown to him by Bashir he had called Jones “a faggot”.

Bashir, when defending Jones in court, has said the allegations against her client were “trial by media” fuelled by hatred and jealousy. Hadley “wanted to destroy” Jones and to “tear him apart”, the barrister has said previously.
Bashir put to Hadley on Wednesday that he was having a difficult time after his secret contract to replace Jones was torn up and Jones was re-signed in May 2019 for two more years.
“Not at all, I maintained the same job I’d done for the previous 17 years and inadvertently Mr Jones had doubled my salary,” Hadley replied.
after newsletter promotion
Hadley disagreed that the pinnacle of his career was attaining the breakfast radio slot, insisting that “going from $2m to $4m” while remaining on the Ray Hadley Morning Show was the pinnacle.
Hadley told the court he was approached by management in late 2018 and they said they’d had enough of Jones and his then-defamation cases and offered him the job.
“I didn’t want to get out of bed at 1.30am, but the money made me do it,” Hadley said.
Bashir suggested to Hadley that a later text to Jones – who was suffering from ill health – was rubbish. It read: “I love you.”
The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.
