articles.title: Could the man who murdered a Christian missionary and his sons walk free in India?
articles.summary: Dara Singh is serving a life sentence for burning alive Graham Staines and his two sons in Odisha in 1999.

blocks.text: Warning: This article contains details of violent death that some readers may find distressing
One of India's most shocking incidents of anti-Christian violence is back in the news more than a quarter of a century after it drew condemnation from around the world.

On Wednesday, the Supreme Court is due to take a call on a petition seeking release from prison by a man, who is convicted of killing Australian Christian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons in 1999.

Dara Singh - whose real name is Rabindra Kumar Pal - has been in jail since his arrest in 2000, serving a life sentence for burning alive the Australian missionary and his six and 10-year-old sons in a village in the eastern state of Odisha (formerly Orissa).

Staines had spent 30 years working with leprosy patients, but Singh and his associates from Hindu hardline groups had accused him of forcibly converting poor Hindus from disadvantaged castes and tribals to Christianity.

The viciousness of the crime sent shockwaves through India's minority Christian community and caused global outrage. Now reports that Singh may be set free have brought alive memories of the heinous crime.
Staines lived in Baripada in Mayurbhanj district, where he worked among the local tribal community.

On the night of their murder on 22 January 1999, Staines and his sons had attended a Christian gathering in Manoharpur, a remote village in the neighbouring district of Keonjhar. They were sleeping in their jeep when a mob of 60 to 70 people led by Singh surrounded their vehicle, set fire to it and prevented them from escaping.

As Singh went on the run after the crime, police put up posters all over the state, offering an 800,000-rupee (approximately $18,000 then) reward for information leading to his capture. Reports at the time said he was helped by villagers and tribals who eulogised him as "a modern-day Tarzan who plays with elephants and rides tigers". He was arrested a year later during an overnight raid on a jungle hideout.

In a sensational interview, external with the India Today magazine's Ruben Banerjee from prison a few months later, he denied killing Staines and his children but said he "did not like Graham Staines" and had "spearheaded the movement against missionaries".

"Missionaries have been targeting our religion. They have been converting Hindus by deceit and inducements. Our religion is under siege. As a true Hindu, it was my responsibility to oppose them," he said. "Since I was possibly the most famous name in the region, the police implicated me in the killings."
Singh added that he was "prepared to be a martyr for the cause of Hindus" but believed that he would never get convicted.

His optimism was misplaced - in 2003, a trial court sentenced Singh to death and 12 others to life imprisonment. Two years later, the high court commuted his death sentence. It confirmed the life term of his accomplice Mahendra Hembram but freed 11 others, saying there was not enough evidence to support their convictions.
In January 2011, the Supreme Court upheld Singh's life sentence, refusing the prosecutors' plea to reinstate the death penalty.

The Staines murder was not the only crime Singh was guilty of. In 2007, he was convicted for two other heinous crimes he committed against religious minorities in 1999 - the same year he murdered the Australian missionary and his children.

He received life sentences, external for leading a mob that set fire to a church and killed Catholic priest Arul Das with an arrow as he tried to flee the burning building and, in the second instance, for beating and burning to death a Muslim garment trader Shaikh Rahaman.

Police had registered 10 cases accusing Singh of involvement in hijacking trucks of Muslim traders transporting cows - an animal many Hindus consider sacred - and setting them free. In his interview, Singh denied being "involved personally", saying "my supporters might have done it". But he admitted that he was "actively involved in the movement against illegal trade in cows and cowslaughter" which "had to be stopped at any cost".

Church leaders had alleged the attacks were carried out at the behest of hardline Hindu organisation Bajrang Dal but Singh denied he was a member and an enquiry commission, led by retired top court judge DP Wadhwa, later ruled that he had worked alone.

Graham Staines' widow, Gladys, who stayed on in India with her daughter Esther until July 2004, said she had "forgiven" Dara Singh in the Christian spirit. "Forgiveness opens up the path of healing," she said.

In July 2024, Singh filed a plea for remission in the top court, saying he was entitled to be released because he had spent more than 25 years in prison. He said his conduct had been good in jail and expressed remorse for his actions.
The 62-year-old blamed the crime on "the fervour of youth" in his petition, external seeking early release.
"The petitioner acknowledges and deeply regrets the transgressions committed more than two decades ago.

"In the fervour of youth, fuelled by impassioned reactions to the brutal history of India, the petitioner's psyche momentarily lost restraint and it is imperative for the court to scrutinise not merely the actions but the underlying intent, noting that there was no personal animosity harboured towards any victim," he wrote.
Last year, the top court asked the state government to take a call on his plea, but the authorities have so far not told the court what they intend to do.
At the last hearing on 19 August, authorities told the court that the Sentence Review Board (SRB), which is examining Singh's plea, was waiting for some more paperwork and sought an adjournment.

The two-judge bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi expressed their annoyance at the several adjournments the state had sought in the case and said if the SRB failed to decide Singh's plea by 2 September, the court would. "You take a decision, whichever way you want. If you do not take a decision, then we will."

Reports that Singh may walk free if the state government or the court accept his remission petition have led to some disquiet in India's 30-million Christian community - some of it because of unease over his earlier statements.

In his 2000 India Today interview, he said he had "no regrets" and "will never regret" killing Staines' children. "When Hindus die, others don't cry. Why should we weep when others die? Whatever has happened is right. Whatever will happen will also be right."
If released from prison, he said, he would "go back to what I have been doing - oppose cow slaughter and conversions".
"The government must stop them. If they are not stopped, more people might get killed. Anything can happen," he added.

In an article on the Union of Catholic News (UCN) website, human rights and Christian political activist John Dayal wrote recently that remission after decades in jail is "not unusual" in India and "the principle behind it - that punishment should allow for reform and eventual return to society - is humane".

But the anxiety among religious minorities in Odisha "is not abstract given the state's history of anti-Christian violence", Dayal points out, citing the Kandhamal riots of 2008, in which dozens were killed and tens of thousands were displaced.

"The Staines murders were not an ordinary homicide but a public, theatrical act of terror, intended to be seen and understood as a warning. The killings of Father Arul Doss and Sheikh Rehman extended that same message," he writes.

"What remains to be seen is not whether Singh will eventually walk free, but how the government conducts itself around that decision...and whether minority communities are given any reassurance," Dayal adds.

articles.title: Two sides in Alberta separation debate entrenched, with majority wanting to remain in Canada: poll
articles.summary: With fewer than 50 days until this October’s referendum, a new poll suggests Albertans remain entrenched in long-held positions tied to the idea of separating from Canada.

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, left, waits to deliver a speech on Alberta Day in Calgary on Aug. 30. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
With fewer than 50 days until this October’s referendum, a new poll suggests Albertans remain entrenched in long-held positions tied to the idea of separating from Canada.
Majority of respondents in favour of immigration reforms in October’s referendum, Research Co. poll says

The Research Co. poll from August found 74 per cent of respondents would vote for Alberta to remain in Canada, while 22 per cent would vote for the Government of Alberta to start the legal process required to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Support for the idea of a binding referendum was highest among Albertans aged 35 to 54, at 27 per cent. Twenty per cent of Albertans aged 55 and older voiced support for a further referendum, while 18 per cent of those aged 18 to 34 agreed with the idea.
Public opinion polls, including for CBC News, have consistently shown a majority of Albertans support staying in Canada.
“Even though we still have a few weeks left to go in this campaign, people seem to be very set in their ways,” Mario Canseco, president of the Vancouver-based polling firm, told CBC News.
“This is definitely not a situation that has winning conditions for the side that wants to separate.”

The results come from an online survey of 750 likely voters in Alberta, conducted by Research Co. between Aug. 24 and 26. The survey has a margin of error of +/- 3.6 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Canseco asks the question around separation about once per year, tracing back to Rachel Notley’s time as Alberta premier. Numbers typically range around 25 to 30 per cent who say they like the idea of secession, he said.

Those numbers track with other polling. In April, a poll directed by Janet Brown Opinion Research for CBC News found 27 per cent said they’d vote for separation, while 67 per cent said they’d vote against it.

items: Support for Alberta separatism flat, struggling high earners more likely supporters: poll
Majority of Albertans would vote to stay in Canada, find Smith's handling poor: poll

blocks.text: With time ticking toward the Oct. 19 referendum vote, federalist and separatist groups have been ramping up their voter mobilization efforts.
But pollsters like Canseco have found there are few who don’t have their minds made up.

“There’s a tiny level of undecideds when we ask about the separation question — only four per cent,” Canseco said of his latest poll’s findings. “Usually, when you have an election or a referendum, the level of undecideds is higher — maybe 10 to 15 per cent.”
Differences on immigration, constitutional reform
Though Research Co. found the idea of holding a binding vote on separation is “not resonating with the public,” the same can’t uniformly be said when it comes to the other ballots.
In addition to the separation question, October’s referendum includes five questions tied to immigration and four to constitutional reform.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: Ranging from 58 to 66 per cent, a majority of likely voters said they would vote “yes” on the five questions related to immigration, according to the poll.

“This is an issue that the government has really connected well on, because you do have people who maybe voted for the NDP in the last election of Alberta, who voted for the Liberals in the last election in Canada, who look at this as an interesting idea,” Canseco said.
The most popular of the proposals is the ballot question asking about requiring proof of citizenship when voting, with 66 per cent support.

On the lower end, 58 per cent said they’d be in favour of a law mandating only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an “Alberta-approved” immigration status would be eligible for provincially-funded programs like health care and education.

items: Immigration is on the ballot. Here’s what some of Alberta’s multicultural communities say about the referendum
What some immigrants could lose if Alberta votes yes to Danielle Smith's questions

blocks.text: The federalist group Alberta's Voice, run by political strategist Stephen Carter, is behind the “no to the nine” signs, encouraging voters to reject the ballot questions.
Carter said he believes people are starting to ask themselves what the nine other questions actually mean, and that will lead to a decline in support leading up to referendum day.
He doesn’t think most Albertans want the government to implement the kinds of policies he believes the questions will lead to.
“I think that as people become more aware of what these actual questions are asking, we’ll see the numbers start to drop,” he said.
“But for now, it’s fairly easy just to say yes to these questions, even while saying no to leaving Canada.”
The Research Co. poll found that public support was lower on the four questions tied to constitutional reform, ranging from 39 to 46 per cent support.

items: Albertans to vote on judicial appointments as premier argues ‘distinct legal traditions’
Once seeking Senate reform, Alberta now ponders voting to be ‘rid of the darn thing’

blocks.text: Tanya Clemens, co-leader of the Alberta independence group Let Alberta Decide, said the higher support for the questions on constitutional reforms — compared to the separation question — shows a gap in understanding what a vote for independence promises to deliver.

“It was close to a majority wanting constitutional changes. I don’t know if they understand that by voting [to remain], it’s basically voting for status quo and for things to stay the same,” Clemens said.
“It doesn’t give Alberta any more leverage. So to me, it looks like there’s some more education that needs to happen.”
The poll also found that likely voters in Alberta thought the validity of the referendum as a “true representation of the wishes of the public” depends on voter turnout.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Joel is a reporter/editor with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca

articles.title: Ariana Grande ends tour and steps back from public life
articles.summary: The star makes an emotional farewell as she wraps up a tour she's described as her "last hurrah".

blocks.text: Ariana Grande made an emotional exit on Tuesday night, as she wrapped up her Eternal Sunshine tour, and prepared to step back from public life.
The singer was occasionally close to tears - most notably during One Last Time, the song that took on extra meaning as an anthem for survivors of the 2017 Manchester terror attack.
"London, I'm going to need you to help me on this one," she said, kneeling down to be near the audience throughout the performance.
Last month, Grande announced a break from all future public-facing appearances following months of intense speculation about her health and appearance.
The step-back includes Grande's withdrawal from a production of Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George at London's Barbican next summer.
She was due to appear alongside her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey. He also pulled out of the production on Tuesday.
On stage in London, Grande showed no signs of fragility or poor health - other than a foot injury that required her to swap her trademark stilettos for a succession of knee-high platform boots.
Nonetheless, she sprang across the stage in sync with her dancers, often on tip-toe to compensate for the lost height of her high heels.
But her composure slipped during the song Nowhere, Nobody, as she sang the line: "Hard to believe in a perfect ending."
The blip was short-lived, though. Professional to the core, Grande was never less than magnetic on stage.

Even before that announcement, Grande had described the Eternal Sunshine tour - which started in the US in June - as "one last hurrah", saying she wanted to take more acting roles after her Oscar-nominated performance in Wicked.
That meant her 10 show residency at London's O2 Arena represented many fans' last chance to see her in concert.
They flew in from all over the world - from China and Australia and cities all across Europe - with 200,000 people attending the London dates alone.
On the second night, Grande surprised the audience by bringing out her Wicked co-star Cynthia Erivo for a rendition of their movie duet For Good.
Across the board, reviews were positive.

"There's no question about it - Ariana Grande is one of the best singers of her generation," wrote Rolling Stone magazine, external, noting that "there were no signs" of the singer "struggling or not wanting to be there".
The Telegraph called the show "flawless", external, praising its "Hollywood-indebted" staging, and Grande's "genuine affection for Britain".
The BBC's review highlighted quieter songs like Imperfect For You, describing them as "delicate and gorgeous and strangely intimate in a room of 20,000 people".

But Guardian writer Kate Solomon said she was "gripped by genuine concern", external for Grande, even when she was enjoying the show, adding: "I really hope this tour does not go down in history for the wrong reasons".
The NME, by contrast, was left breathless by the star's physical prowess.
"Throughout the show," marvelled Nick Levine, external, "she skips across the stage in skyscraper heels that most drag performers would baulk at."
That wasn't the case on the final night, however, due to what Grande described as a "deep cut" on her foot.
Writing on Instagram, she assured fans the injury wasn't serious, insisting she was "on the mend" and would complete her final shows "even if I am a few inches shorter than usual".
She did so with a huge smile spread across her face, leaning into the big notes of Dangerous Woman, and sprinting across the stage during Break Free - one of many up-tempo highlights.
She ended the show as she always does - attached to a harness, ascending into the rafters of the O2 and disappearing.
Fans were left wondering when, if ever, they'd see her perform again.

articles.title: DOT eyes more visa-free gateways for Chinese tourists
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Spurred by a surge in Chinese tourist arrivals following relaxed visa rules, the Department of Tourism (DOT) is pushing to expand the 14-day visa-free scheme beyond the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Spurred by a surge in Chinese tourist arrivals following relaxed visa rules, the Department of Tourism (DOT) is pushing to expand the 14-day visa-free scheme beyond the country’s main gateways to draw more visitors to secondary destinations.

Tourism Secretary Dita Angara-Mathay said that aside from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (Naia) in Metro Manila and Mactan-Cebu International Airport in Cebu, the DOT wants the visa-free arrangement extended to other gateways serving major tourist destinations, including Clark, Caticlan, Palawan and Bohol, among others.

“If we’re going to get all the other agencies to sign up on this, then we can expect a lot more charter flights from China and a lot more arrivals,” Angara-Mathay said on the sidelines of the DOT’s partnership renewal with online booking platform Klook on Tuesday.

According to her, the DOT has prepared a position paper laying out the economic case for the expansion, backed by statistical analysis showing what she described as the “profound effect” of easier visa access on Philippine tourism.
Booming Chinese arrivals

Based on preliminary eTravel registrations, China recorded the biggest jump in tourist arrivals from January to August, with 310,088 visitors so far this year, up 69.15 percent year-on-year—an increase that the DOT chief said strengthens the case for expanding the visa-free arrangement.
“Can you imagine if you expand to cover more areas?” Angara-Mathay said.
That made China the country’s fourth-largest source of foreign visitors behind the United States, South Korea and Japan.

Overall, the Philippines recorded about 4.11 million arrivals as of Aug. 31 based on eTravel data. The DOT is targeting between 6.4 million and 6.8 million arrivals this year, although Angara-Mathay said reaching 7 million remains possible.
“It looks like, and we might just be sure to hit this target. And even more, especially if we’re able to get more tourist arrivals from target markets,” she said.
Secondary cities push
Apart from expanding visa-free entry, the DOT is pushing for more air links between secondary cities in the Philippines and key overseas markets, according to Tourism Assistant Secretary Ren Sapitan.
Tourism Undersecretary Stanley Ng, a former Philippine Airlines president, has been leading talks with carriers on potential new services, particularly involving China and South Korea.

Rather than concentrating connectivity on major hubs such as Seoul, the DOT wants airlines to explore secondary cities abroad and link them through charter flights to Philippine destinations such as Bohol and Caticlan. /cb

articles.title: ‘Foreign malign influence’ going ‘street level’ – AFP
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — “Foreign malign influence (FMI)” operations targeting the Philippines are adopting a more “street-level” approach, using the Filipino language to integrate themselves into…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — “Foreign malign influence (FMI)” operations targeting the Philippines are adopting a more “street-level” approach, using the Filipino language to integrate themselves into divisive domestic issues and thus becoming harder to detect, a military official said on Tuesday.

Reservist Rear Adm. Roy Vincent Trinidad, the Armed Forces of the Philippines spokesperson on the West Philippine Sea (WPS), said the shift became apparent in the “first quarter” of the year, as the WPS maritime issue became linked to other local controversies.

The intended discourse “used to be clearly identifiable as pro-Davao [when it comes to] West Philippine Sea issues,” Trinidad said in a press briefing. But “today, the formalized influence approach is they meddle with local issues.”

He cited the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the flood control scandal, and criticism against President Marcos and Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. among the issues the AFP is monitoring for possible FMIs.
Raid on Chinese-run firm
One local issue which, he said, has been exploited by foreign propaganda is the May 15 raid on Chinese-run Philippine Sanjia Steel Corp.

The raid at an ecozone in Misamis Oriental led to the arrest of 69 Chinese nationals and the discovery of radioactive materials in the Sanjia plant. The Chinese Embassy at the time filed a diplomatic protest over the arrests.
Trinidad said “It is now more difficult to detect [foreign influence] because it is already mixing with local issues.”
He also said the language “now is [more] prevalent in Tagalog,” whereas “before, it was mostly in English.”
“Attacks on the SND (secretary of national defense), attacks on [Rear Adm.] Jay Tarriela are now in Tagalog,” Trinidad noted. Tarriela serves as Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson on WPS issues.
He also noted a shift in language among officials of the Chinese Embassy.
“When it’s the deputy spokesperson of the Chinese Embassy, they use Tagalog and street-level [phrasing]. When it’s the spokesman of the Chinese Embassy, his tone is diplomatic,” Trinidad said.
This shift to a more informal messaging may be part of efforts to make social-media content harder to identify as foreign and more acceptable to Filipinos, Trinidad said.
“Definitely, this is part of their approach. They are adjusting to make it more acceptable to our fellow countrymen, so they can conceal it better,” he said.
In an advice to netizens encountering such content, he said: “Before ‘liking,’ before forwarding, before clicking, make sure carefully if what you are reading is true.” /cb

articles.title: Remarkable US oil deal puzzles analysts - and angers many Venezuelans
articles.summary: Amounting to 65 billion barrels of crude, the deal is labelled by one ex-envoy as a colonialist "fever dream".

blocks.text: From the moment elite US troops swooped into Nicolás Maduro's compound in Caracas to forcibly remove him from power in January, President Donald Trump made clear that securing control over Venezuela's oil resources was a key goal of his administration.
The United States would "run" Venezuela, he said at the time, and manage the sale of Venezuelan oil for the foreseeable future.

The signing of a huge US-Venezuela oil deal in Caracas on Wednesday marks the fruition of that plan. The agreement grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela, amounting to a staggering 65 billion barrels of crude. That equates to more than a fifth of the country's proven oil reserves.
Beyond the eye-watering numbers, both sides heralded the deal as good for their respective nations.

President Trump called it "the biggest oil deal in world history", while the interim Venezuelan President, Delcy Rodríguez, said the agreement was "historic", and would generate $100bn (£74bn) in investment and more than $200bn in tax revenue.
Others profoundly disagreed.

"This is a terrible deal. [Rodríguez] has given away 20% of the national patrimony for nothing," said Trump's former special representative on Venezuela and Iran, Elliott Abrams. "I think she is simply complying with the demands she's getting from Washington."

On Tuesday, the White House released a fact sheet which set out some details of the deal's framework. The US government will work alongside a private business in Venezuela called North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep), the second largest private oil producer in Venezuela after Chevron.

One extraordinary detail of how the Trump administration will work with Nabep is that the US government will have "veto power over the appointment of any member of the board of directors, and a majority of Nabep's board of directors must be US citizens".
With the ongoing US war with Iran increasing prices at the petrol pumps, a boost in oil production outside of the Middle East could affect consumers.

Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum told Fox Business the pact was "shifting the geopolitical centre of the global energy markets" away from what he called the "choke points in the Middle East" and back to the Western Hemisphere.

There is a logic to the US-Venezuela partnership, Elliott Abrams argued, while Gulf oil supplies are currently so unreliable. But he said the terms are so one-sided they are a "kind of fever dream of what colonialism looks like".

The White House has spoken of the deal having "re-established the Monroe Doctrine", an 18th Century principle exerting US power across South America - "purging foreign malign influence from our backyard and ensuring American dominance in our hemisphere is never again questioned".
Despite the insistence from both governments that the plan will benefit both Venezuelans and Americans, it is not without pitfalls and clear unanswered questions.

The proposed timeframe alone is problematic. Trump has said the agreement will generate profit within two or three years. Energy experts, however, warn the dire state of the Venezuelan oil sector means a decade is more realistic.

Luis Pacheco, of the Baker Institute at Rice University in Houston, told BBC Mundo that Venezuela needs to invest about $100bn over eight years in order to return to its oil production levels of 30 years ago.
"It's important to know who will manage those resources and for what purpose," Pacheco said.

"Are they going to put the same people in charge of managing that money who already squandered the biggest oil boom of the century?" he asked, referring to past mismanagement of the country's oil wealth.
The Venezuelan opposition is concerned the deal deepens President Trump's relationship with Delcy Rodríguez, whom they accuse of heading the same regime as Maduro.
The Trump administration not only decried Maduro's government as a corrupt drug cartel, but surrounded Venezuela with the biggest armada of the modern era.
The ease and speed with which Washington has now pivoted to working with Maduro's former vice-president infuriates the opposition.

The Nobel Peace Prize winner and presidential hopeful, María Corina Machado, may choose not to publicly criticise President Trump, whose support she needs if she hopes to come to power. Others, though, have been more forthcoming.

"You chose to use the power of the United States not to liberate Venezuelans, but to ally yourself with our oppressors," said Venezuelan economist, Ricardo Hausmann, on social media, directing his comments at the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"You opted to push through an asset seizure, an unconstitutional agreement with an illegitimate and oppressive government, instead of using the leadership of the United States to first restore constitutional order and democracy," he said.
The lack of an imminent election in Venezuela – or, indeed, any clear plan towards one – strikes many opponents as a betrayal.

There is betrayal felt at the other end of the ideological spectrum, too. Although the governing socialist party, PSUV, has backed Rodríguez over the US deal, many Venezuelan socialists see it as capitulation.
After almost three decades opposing Washington's influence in the region, they feel she has gifted the country's most valuable asset to the old enemy.

The deal "hands over [the oil] and opens the doors to a new colonialism of the United States," said Rafael Ramírez, who served as the head of the state-run energy firm, PDVSA, and as the oil minister under former President Hugo Chávez.
In early 2008, Chávez presented his Sunday television programme, Aló Presidente, from former ExxonMobil oilfields in the Orinoco River Belt.
Having expropriated some of the oil company's assets in the region, he was in a defiant mood.

"We have the reins in our hands and we won't ever let them go again," he said of the state-run oil company's ownership of oilfields, and denounced how previous Washington-friendly governments had turned Venezuela into "a nation of gringos".
"It was a theft of our nation but the Bolivarian Revolution has put a stop to it," he thundered to applause from PDVSA employees.
Yet it was one of his disciples – his handpicked successor's successor – who has now signed this opaque deal with Washington and praised it as a victory for Venezuela.

articles.title: Thieves steal $70,000 worth of beer
articles.summary: MONTCLAIR, California — Thieves made off with tens of thousands of cans of Pabst beer in two separate heists from a Southern California warehouse on the same day, police said. Pabst Blue Ribbon has…

blocks.text: MONTCLAIR, California — Thieves made off with tens of thousands of cans of Pabst beer in two separate heists from a Southern California warehouse on the same day, police said.

Pabst Blue Ribbon has turned the thefts—valued by police at $70,000—into a light-hearted social media promotion. But police in Montclair said on Friday that investigators are trying to determine whether they were part of a single operation.
In the first heist, about $45,000 worth of beer headed to Tucson, Arizona, was picked up but never delivered, according to police.

An hour later, a “purported subcontracting company” submitted fake documents to pick up another $25,000 worth of beer, Montclair police said in a news release. Both thefts occurred on Aug. 17 at an Anheuser-Busch distribution center about 65 kilometers east of Los Angeles.
Roughly 34,000 cans of Pabst Blue Ribbon and non-alcoholic Old Milwaukee beer—more than 1,500 cases—were stolen, according to a police report obtained by the Los Angeles Times.
In Instagram posts, Pabst put the weight of the stolen cargo at 18,145 kilograms and started a countdown seeking its return.

“To the thief: we don’t fault you for wanting to brag to your friends how much PBR you have, we just wish you obtained it the honorable way,” the company wrote. It added, “P.s. this is real and we are deadly serious.” /cb

articles.title: Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up
articles.summary: Explosions have been reported around the Strait of Hormuz, including at an airport in southern Iran. US President Donald Trump said the strikes were a response to Iranian attempts to mine the strait.…

image.caption: The US military announced it had launched strikes on targets in Iran [FILE: August 2026]Image: US Central Command/X

blocks.text: Albanese announces $600m package to combat drug smuggling in Pacific
Australia will step up its support to fight trans-national drug trafficking flowing through the Pacific, with a $600m package.
Anthony Albanese announced the new investment at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, which aims to stop the contraband arriving in Australia.
The increase in drug flow across the Pacific is a huge problem in several countries: linked to increased gang activity in Samoa and Tonga, and a sharp rise in the HIV rate in Fiji.
Heightened activity is showing up in Australian Federal Police interventions of narcotics in the region.
In 2025, about 4.6 tonnes of illicit drugs were seized by local and international law enforcement, the Australian Federal Police reported.
In the first five months of this year, 17 tonnes have been picked up - mostly cocaine.
The new package – which will be opt-in for Pacific countries – will include enhanced aerial surveillance, and police and border training.
“Drug trafficking is having a devastating impact on Pacific communities,” Pacific minister Pat Conroy said.
“This initiative responds to the calls of regional leaders to do more, and to step up regional coordination to address this scourge.”
Key events

blocks.text: Chanel Contos to call for social media opt-in algorithm

blocks.caption: Achol Arok

blocks.text: Achol Arok
Consent education advocate Chanel Contos will urge Australia to enforce a social media opt-in algorithm to help reduce the influence of the “manosphere” on both men and women.
Contos will deliver a speech about the harms of social media algorithms in Australia in an address to the National Press Club in Canberra at midday.
Contos is expected to say:

double quotation markThis is crucial, and the detail in any reform will determine its success – as will be the overall strength of the proposed Digital Duty of Care reforms that are needed in their own right. It is too easy for Big Tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform but actually suit them just fine.

blocks.caption: Chanel Contos will speak at the National Press Club in Canberra at midday today.  Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP

blocks.text: The Teach Us Consent CEO will point to examples of algorithmic harms such as the “manosphere”, accusing bad actors of jumping on to “a market opportunity” that has misogyny “at the heart of its business model”.

double quotation markIt usually starts with something as harmless as a workout video, or motivational content. Very quickly, boys and men are taken into the “manosphere”, communities that persistently promote the idea that emotional control, material wealth, and physical appearance and dominance, especially over women, are markers of male worth. This is harmful to the individual man consuming this content, and then anyone else close to him in life, including other men, but disproportionately women and girls.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.

articles.title: Briton among 119 more people rescued in Nepal after flash floods
articles.summary:
More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000 still missing in disaster triggered by glacial collapse

A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an…

blocks.text: A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an official said almost a week after deadly flash floods on the country’s border with Tibet.
An army spokesperson told reporters at a press conference that Tuesday’s rescue efforts had saved 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.
“We have also rescued one British male during this search and rescue operation, and the search and rescue operation is continuing,” he said.
The British man is yet to be identified. The UK Foreign Office was contacted for comment.
The rescues mark a rare breakthrough in a devastating week for Himalayan communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border.
At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.
Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.

The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.
Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.
Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region.
“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.

A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.
The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.
Scientists have said such disasters are more likely as the climate crisis affects mountainous and polar regions.
The UN’s top scientific advisory body said in 2023 that previously ice-bound landmasses – such as permafrost tundra and mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.
Officials from Nepal, China and Tibet met in May to discuss strengthening their joint response to floods, weather and glacier-related hazards, Reuters reported on Tuesday.

articles.title: Iran: US launches fresh strikes as hostilities flare again
articles.summary: Explosions were reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz, as well as at an airport in southern Iran. US President Trump described the strikes as "large and powerful." Iran said the US will…

image.caption: US President Trump described the strikes as "large and powerful." Iran said the US will "regret" its latest attacks.Image: U.S. Navy/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz flared up again on Tuesday evening as the United States launched fresh strikes on Iranian targets in and around the strategic waterway.

"Explosions were heard again in Bandar Abbas city and Qeshm island," Iranian state television reported, adding that blasts were also heard on Lavan island, home to one of Iran's Gulf oil export terminals.
Oil prices rose in the wake of the latest attacks with US crude up by as much as 5%.

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."

US President Donald Trump said the strikes, which he described as "large and powerful," were retaliation for "failed" Iranian attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz and the firing of "eight missiles" towards a US military base in Jordan, all of which he claimed were shot down.

"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump wrote in his latest social media threat. "But it will not be the biggest attack of them all. That is waiting in the wings."
Iran: IRGC vows to respond to US strikes

An IRGC spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, about 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's joint military command said its armed forces would deliver what they described as "crushing and devastating blows" against the US, while state media said the army had launched operations against unspecified US targets in the region.

The Tasnim news agency said a "decisive operation by Iran's armed forces in response to the US enemy has begun. The US bases and interests in the region are being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones."
G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran
Meanwhile, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.
"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.
"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."
He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with the IRGC.
"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."
Iran's Pezeshkian meets Putin

The latest flare-up comes just hours after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said earlier on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate any US move that signals a return to the collapsed interim ceasefire deal.

Pezeshkian, speaking after the US and Iran had already resumed exchanges of fire for the first time in over a month, accused Washington of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms.
Pezeshkian was speaking on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he also met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday.
Putin reportedly told Pezeshkian that Russia stood in solidarity with Iran, and that the two countries would maintain their economic relationships despite the current turbulence.
Pezeshkian thanked Putin and criticized the US for having "no right" to impose sanctions on other countries.

articles.title: Ed Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward Israel
articles.summary:
Foreign secretary tells MPs he will try to stop illegal settlements carving up the West Bank

Ed Miliband has promised to “reset” Britain’s policy on Israel, saying he will try to stop…

blocks.text: Ed Miliband has promised to “reset” Britain’s policy on Israel, saying he will try to stop British companies helping build settlements in the West Bank.

Speaking to the Commons for the first time as foreign secretary, Miliband said he would set out measures to prevent UK involvement in projects such as the illegal E1 plan, which critics say would split the West Bank in half.
Tuesday’s comments came after Israel issued tenders for around a third of the 3,400 homes planned for the project. Miliband called the settlement “the crossing of a red line”.

He said: “It cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable. This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution. We will act, and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks.
“I want a comprehensive reset of our approach on these issues because it is necessary, it is high time.”
Ministers have been under pressure for weeks to place tighter sanctions on Israel, specifically in relation to the E1 plan.
Last month, Israel invited companies to bid for contracts to build 1,200 homes for the project between East Jerusalem and the settlement of Ma’ale Adumim.

blocks.caption: Ma’ale Adumim in the E1 area of the occupied West Bank, where the Israeli government plans to build thousands of homes. Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/Shutterstock

blocks.text: A group of former British diplomats called on the government in May to threaten action against any companies bidding to build any illegal settlement “designed to divide the West Bank in two and destroy Palestine’s viability”. They warned that E1 was part of Israel’s “systemic West Bank annexation”.
Other governments have condemned the project. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz – usually one of Israel’s staunchest defenders – called it a “big mistake”.
The UK joined a group of 20 other countries, including France, Germany and Italy, as well as the European Union, to issue a joint statement calling E1 “unacceptable”.

The statement said: “The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank and harming the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian territories.”
Miliband said: “We need to look, and we are looking indeed, at our wider economic relationship with the occupied territories and the different tools we have to tackle it.
after newsletter promotion

“I want to be very clear: we do not want British companies financing, constructing, or advertising new settlements. The work we are now undertaking is how we can stop that. And as I say, I’ll have more to say soon.”
Ministers are under pressure to go further and ban trade in goods and services with people or organisations linked to illegal settlements.

James Naish, the Labour MP for Rushcliffe in Nottinghamshire, said: “Does the foreign secretary accept that this pace of expansion shows that current UK measures are failing to change Israeli government behaviour, and that a trade ban is now the necessary next step?”

Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, indicated this could be included in the government’s measures. He said: “We have absolutely condemned the settler violence, the settler terrorism that we have seen, absolutely our condemnation of the proposals for E1 and all illegal settlements, and indeed we have joined other countries around the world in condemning this proposal and been very, very clear with the government of Israel that this must stop.

“The prime minister has been very clear that we need to do more, including looking at further sanctions, both those involved in the violence in Gaza, but also looking at measures to ban trade in goods with illegal settlements.”

The Israeli embassy to London responded by referring to previous comments by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools. The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”

articles.title: US launches new airstrikes on Iranian targets as hostilities flare
articles.summary: Move from Washington quashes hopes that exchange of fire last weekend might not presage ⁠wider renewal of hostilities

blocks.text: The US launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets on Tuesday, quashing hopes that an exchange of fire last ⁠weekend might not presage a ⁠wider renewal of hostilities.

Oil prices had ​already risen after that first exchange of direct attacks since July and after reports of two tankers being hit leaving the strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping.

Tehran remained defiant, warning ⁠that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the renewed Iranian strikes, and a warning from Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, that Washington was about to ⁠impose new sanctions.

“Today at 12 p.m. ET (1600 GMT), U.S. forces began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran,” US Central Command posted on X. “The strikes follow ​recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of ‌Hormuz and against American service members deployed to ‌the region.”
Iran’s state broadcaster said there had been reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait.
The state-linked news agency Nour ‌News said there had been reports of explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast.

The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US airbases in Jordan.

Although he warned of a US response to the Iranian strikes, the US president also told reporters on Monday that they did not signal a return to full-scale war, and a senior Iranian source told Reuters they were a “limited ‌and contained confrontation”.

However, Trump made dire threats against Tehran on social media. He warned that if Iran retaliates against the US’s latest strikes, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.

The ominous last part of Trump’s message was starkly reminiscent of threats the US president has made in the past that could amount to war crimes if carried out, including threatening to destroy critical civilian infrastructure such as power plants and bridges, threatening to bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages”, and an April threat that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if a peace deal wasn’t reached.
In Iran, the Fars news agency quoted an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks”.

More recently pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.

Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, had said early on Tuesday ​that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was intended to halt the conflict.

The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on 28 February. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period – which passed without further agreement.

“I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the ⁠memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, at ​a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which includes Russia ​and China.
But Iranian officials have shown no public ​sign of bowing to pressure.

“If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be ​able to export oil,” Mohammad Baqer QalibafIran’s parliament speaker was ​quoted as saying by Iranian media. If ​the US intensified its “siege”, he said Tehran would respond militarily.
Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was “addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”.

“As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far,” he added, warning that Tehran would “use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus”.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
articles.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 6,000 confirmed cases, with nearly 3,000 deaths. As the virus spreads, authorities are racing to contain one of the deadliest…

image.caption: The Ebola outbreak has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain itImage: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it.

"Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance," DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo.
"Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control," he added.
Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities.
Ebola outbreak in DR Congo outpaces efforts to contain it

"This outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it, but it can be stopped," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told journalists last week.
The United Nations has appealed for more funding as humanitarian agencies struggle to keep pace with the increasing number of cases.

"International attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground," Guterres said, warning that the world "must also overcome another virus — the virus of indifference."
Vaccination campaign gathers momentum
As researchers continue trials aimed at developing a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain, Congolese authorities have rolled out a vaccination campaign focused on front-line health workers.
The vaccine was originally developed for a different Ebola variant, but officials hope it will provide some protection against the current outbreak.
Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses had already arrived in the country.

"We will cover all the provinces that are around Ituri, moving in a ring towards the center of the outbreak, that is to say towards Ituri. But we have enough doses for all healthcare providers," he said on August 28.
Some health workers remain confident despite uncertainty over how effective the vaccine will be against the Bundibugyo strain.

"It is a vaccine that has already proven itself. We are talking about Ebola Bundibugyo, of Ugandan origin. But the vaccine that they want to administer to us was the vaccine that had succeeded for the Zaire type," said health worker Arnaud Batumbu.
"Since both cases involve a viral disease, I hope the vaccine will work for us now as well," he added.
Communities seek protection
Residents in hard-hit areas say they are ready to take the vaccine if it is properly explained to them.
"I will be ready to get vaccinated if only someone explains to me the importance of this vaccination," Clemency, a student in Tshopo province, told DW.

blocks.caption: Health workers are worried about the spread of the virusImage: Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Others are calling for wider access. "Children need to be vaccinated too. They go back to school; there are many of them in class," said local resident Carine Lobwadji
Some community members also fear vaccine supplies may not be enough.

"I have learned that this is an insufficient quantity. I ask the authorities to add other doses for Tshopo and that we vaccinate everyone, especially those who will voluntarily agree, since some are afraid," said Onyeka Treasure, a photographer.
Violence hampers response
The latest outbreak is unfolding against a backdrop of violence and mass displacement in eastern DRC, complicating efforts to stop transmission.
Ebola response teams have reported attacks while carrying out their work, including during operations to safely handle Ebola-related deaths.

"We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives," Floribert Magene, a member of an Ebola response team, told The Associated Press on Monday after an attack in Ituri province.
Magene said his team was assaulted near Mambasa while responding to a call to secure a body.
Economic toll grows
Beyond the health emergency, the outbreak is worsening economic hardship for many families.
Schools have reopened in towns such as Bukavu and Bunia, but many parents are struggling to afford basic school supplies.
DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts
Stationery shop owner Furaha Mpangu Esperance told DW that demand has collapsed as families prioritize food and other essentials.

"In any case, it doesn't work. The situation is serious because there are no customers. We have even lowered the prices but there is no one to buy. Before, we even sold 10 boxes, 20 boxes a day. Today not even three boxes, not even two! The situation is critical," he said.
To reduce disruption to education, the government has proposed radio-based learning for children unable to attend school.

"For us, it's a double objective: to ensure that children continue to go to school, despite the epidemic, and to ensure that distance learning is the device that will help them," Education Minister Raissa Malu told DW.

blocks.caption: Schools have enforced protective measures, like hand-washingImage: DW

blocks.text: Teachers, however, say many areas lack the infrastructure needed for effective distance learning.

"We, the teachers, are ready, but we don't have the tools. In sensitive areas, even picking up frequencies is quite a problem," said Patrick Girinegi, president of the Ituri teachers' inter-union alliance. "The first-grade children can't read, nor do the parents. Several schools don't have printers or computers. How will it go?"
Many students and parents would rather see classrooms remain open with stronger health measures in place.

"It's easy for me to understand when it's my teacher himself who explains it to me. Saying that the child stays at home to listen to the radio, I don't think it's going to work. We [must] find ways to go to school without contaminating ourselves," said Viviane Tshipamba, vice-president of the Ituri children's committee.

Despite the challenges, health authorities point to a positive sign: more than 1,360 people have recovered from Ebola so far. For many Congolese, those recoveries offer hope that with stronger support, increased vaccination rates and improved security, the outbreak can still be brought under control.
Marcus Loika, Gaston Mukendi and Mitima Delachance contributed to this article.

articles.title: ‘Where’s Newfoundland?’ ask shocked residents looking at Hilroy exercise books
articles.summary: As a new school year approaches, parents and students are out buying new school supplies — but one classroom staple has people in Newfoundland and Labrador demanding answers.

image.caption: Hilroy Canada's glossy exercise books don't include Newfoundland or Cape Breton on the cover. (Elizabeth Whitten/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
As a new school year approaches, parents and students are out buying new school supplies — but one classroom staple has people in Newfoundland and Labrador demanding answers.
New design is missing Newfoundland, Cape Breton

Hilroy Canada exercise books are known for the map of Canada on the cover. The design for a glossy version of the notebook also features the map but it's missing some of Canada’s geographical features — namely Newfoundland and Cape Breton.
When handed a book by CBC News, Victor Aucoin, a teacher, initially admired the design but on closer inspection asked, “Where’s Newfoundland?” before laughing.
“There’s no Newfoundland. Oh, so we don’t exist in Canada, OK! That’s nice to see,” he said.
“The most beautiful island on Earth and… we didn’t make it to Canada,” he added, shaking his head a little. “What a sin.”
Aucoin said given the province's economic importance to the country, it was shocking to see the island missing, adding he won’t be buying these books.
“I know in my classroom if some children come in, I will ask them to tell their parents to contact Hilroy and file a complaint, as I will as well.”
He added his mother is from Cape Breton.
“Wait till I call her and tell her Cape Breton is no longer part of Canada. She’s going to be pleased. No Newfoundland. No Cape Breton,” he said, again shaking his head.
Aucoin reiterated the situation is unacceptable and he would be contacting the company to tell them to take the new exercise books off the shelves.
“This is an uproar.”
It's not clear when the design was released. CBC News has contacted ACCO Brands, which owns Hilroy, for an interview but did not hear back by publication.
‘It’s bananas’
Johnathan Goodyear, also looking over the new design, said it was “kind of crazy” that Newfoundland is missing and wondered how it happened. He’d like to see the company recall the exercise books.
“It’s bananas," he said.
Goodyear added Newfoundland and Labrador has contributed a lot to Canada, especially on a military front, so “knocking us off is pretty rough.”
Some people worried the omission could have a detrimental impact on students learning about the country.
Goodyear is concerned it could leave students unaware of the country’s geography.
“It’s kind of a big deal.”
Rose Wilkinson said Newfoundland should be included in the cover and worries people don’t know where Newfoundland is.
“I feel like most people don’t think of it as a place [in] Canada because it’s so small," she said.
Dace Gruchy, who initially admired the new design for its bright colours, was also unimpressed when he noticed Newfoundland was missing from the cover.
“That’s mad disrespectful," said Gruchy. “We should be on this ‘cause we’re part of Canada.”
